The evaluator-optimizer loop from Module 06 is the same machinery pointed inward at generation time rather than at CI; we connect them but don’t re-teach orchestration.

133.title: 1. Why your testing intuition breaks
133.content: Let’s be specific about what a unit test assumes, because every assumption is about to fail. A unit test asserts that f(x) == expected. For this to be a useful, stable test, four things must hold: f is deterministic (same x, same output); there is a single correct expected; correctness is binary (equal or not); and f’s dependencies are pinned (nothing changes underneath without a version bump you control). For an agent built on an LLM, all four fail at once. Nondeterminism: same input, different output. Call the model twice with identical inputs and you get two different completions. Sampling is probabilistic; even at temperature=0 you are not guaranteed bit-identical output across requests, because batching, hardware, and kernel nondeterminism leak through. So assert agent(task) == expected is not occasionally flaky — it is categorically the wrong shape. There is no single output to assert against. Your CI mental model — green is green, red is red, a flake is a bug to be fixed — assumes determinism that does not exist here. A test that passes 80% of the time isn’t a broken test; it’s an accurate measurement of an 80%-reliable behavior, and the information is in the 80%, not in the pass/fail of any single run. No single correct answer: a space, not a point. Ask Scout to “summarize this incident report” and there is no canonical string. There is a region of acceptable summaries — many phrasings, lengths, and emphases that a competent human would call correct — surrounded by a region of unacceptable ones (missed the root cause, hallucinated a service name, three paragraphs of fluff). Equality is meaningless. The question is never “does the output equal X” but “does the output land inside the acceptable region,” and that region is defined by properties, not by a golden string. Continuous quality: better and worse, not pass and fail. Two summaries can both be acceptable while one is clearly better. Quality is a scalar — frequently a fuzzy, human-judgment scalar — not a boolean. A prompt change might move average quality from 7.2 to 7.6 on some rubric. There is no unit-test vocabulary for “got somewhat better.” Your suite needs to express distributions over a quality scale, and to tell a real 0.4 improvement from noise. Dependency drift — “prompt rot”: the one that should scare you most. In a normal service, dependencies are pinned. requests==2.31.0 behaves identically today and next year; an upgrade is an explicit, reviewable diff, and if it breaks an interface the compiler or type checker tells you at build time. The model is a dependency with none of these properties. The provider ships claude-sonnet-4-6 → claude-sonnet-4-7 and your behavior shifts — usually better, sometimes subtly worse on your specific prompts, which were implicitly tuned against quirks of the old version. Your code did not change. Your tests (if you wrote unit tests) still pass, because they assert on your code, not on model behavior. There is no compiler, no type system, no failing build to catch a model upgrade silently changing what your agent does. This is the deepest reason agents need evals: they are the only mechanism that turns “the model changed” from an invisible, existential risk into a visible, measured diff. 📖 The term prompt rot names the slow divergence between a prompt and the model it was tuned against. Your prompt is a contract co-evolved with a specific model’s behavior. Upgrade the model and the contract is silently renegotiated. Without an eval suite you find out from a user, in production, weeks later. So unit testing is the wrong tool — not because testing is wrong but because its assumptions don’t hold. What does hold its assumptions? Benchmarking and statistics. You don’t ask “is this one output correct.” You run a population of tasks many times and score the results statistically — distributions, rates, confidence intervals. You stop thinking like someone asserting equality and start thinking like someone running an A/B test or a clinical trial: measuring a noisy effect against a baseline and asking whether the difference is real. That mental shift is the whole module. Everything below is mechanics in service of it. ✅ The reframe in one line. Unit testing asks “is this output correct?” Evaluation asks “across a representative population of tasks, run enough times, how often does my agent land in the acceptable region — and is that rate meaningfully different from my baseline?” .

134.title: 2. Eval vs benchmark
134.content: These words get used interchangeably and they should not be. The distinction determines which question you’re answering. A benchmark is the standardized, shared, leaderboard kind of eval. SWE-bench, GPQA, MMLU, τ-bench. A fixed dataset, a fixed grader, published so everyone scores the same way. Its purpose is to compare models on a common axis — it’s how you read “the new model is 12 points better at agentic coding.” Benchmarks are public goods: they let the whole field talk about capability in shared units. An eval is any measurement of system quality. Usually private and bespoke to your task — your cases, your grader, your definition of “good.” Its purpose is to answer “does my system do my job well enough to ship?” . The clean way to hold the relationship: all benchmarks are evals; most evals are not benchmarks. A benchmark is the special case of an eval that has been standardized and shared for cross-model comparison. The two answer different questions and you need both: . | Benchmarks → model selection. “Is Opus or Sonnet better at the kind of work Scout does?” Read public benchmarks for a first cut, then confirm on your own eval — see below for why you can’t stop at the benchmark. | Private evals → does my system work. No public benchmark measures whether Scout resolves your customers’ tickets. Only a private eval built from your tasks does. This is the one you actually gate ships on. | . Three reasons you cannot outsource your judgment to public benchmarks: . | Contamination. Benchmarks leak into training data. A model scoring well on SWE-bench may have seen SWE-bench tasks. The score conflates capability with memorization, and you can’t tell the ratio from outside. | Goodhart’s law. “When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.” Public benchmarks are targets the entire industry optimizes toward. Models get tuned to them, which inflates scores relative to the messy real tasks the benchmark was meant to proxy. | Construct-validity gap. A benchmark measures a proxy for what you care about. SWE-bench measures “resolves GitHub issues in these 12 Python repos.” That is genuinely informative and genuinely not your codebase, your stack, your bug distribution, your definition of an acceptable fix. | . This is why your private eval suite is a strategic asset — a moat. Anyone can read the same public leaderboard. The thing competitors cannot copy is your curated set of your real tasks with your graders, accumulated from your production failures. It is the most durable artifact in your whole agent stack: models churn, frameworks churn, but a well-curated eval suite compounds in value every month you feed it. Treat it like production code, because it is.

135.title: 3. The anatomy of an eval
135.content: Every eval, from a one-off script to a 5,000-case suite, has the same three parts. Get all three right or the number lies to you. Dataset (what to test on) → Grader (how to score one run) → Aggregation (how to turn many noisy scores into a decision) . 3a. The dataset — cases, but a “case” is a whole world . A case is one task you grade the agent on. For a prompt eval, a case is an input and a grading key. For an agent, a case is heavier: it is an entire environment / fixture — a directory of files, a seeded database, mocked tool responses, an initial state — because an agent acts on an environment, not just responds to a string. “Fix the failing test in this repo” only means something if “this repo” is a concrete, frozen tree of files. Two properties make a dataset trustworthy: . | Frozen and reproducible. A case must produce the same starting world every single time you run it, on any machine, today and in six months. If the fixture drifts — a file edited in place, a date that depends on now(), a network call to a live service — your eval measures the drift, not the agent. Freeze the fixture; copy it fresh for each trial (we do exactly this in the exercise). | Tagged for slicing. Each case carries metadata: category (bugfix / extraction / qa), difficulty, source, whatever cleaves your task space. You almost never want one aggregate number; you want per-slice numbers, because “82% overall” can hide “bugfix collapsed from 90% to 60% while extraction rose and masked it.” Tags are how you see the collapse. | . Where cases come from — three sources, and the order matters: . | Hand-authored seeds. You sit down and write the obvious tasks the agent must handle. This bootstraps the suite and encodes your spec. It is also where every suite starts and where weak suites stop. | Production-mined failures — the flywheel, and the most valuable source by far. Every time Scout fails in production — an escalation, a human correction, a thumbs-down, a reverted commit — you freeze that exact situation as a new case with the correct outcome as its grading key. Now it is a permanent regression test. The agent can never silently re-break it. This is the engine that makes an eval suite a moat: it grows from reality, automatically covering the failures that actually happen rather than the ones you imagined. A team with a disciplined flywheel pulls away from one without it every single week. | Synthetic and adversarial. Use a model to generate cases — permute parameters, manufacture edge cases, write deliberately nasty inputs (injection attempts, contradictory instructions, empty files, enormous files). Cheap breadth, but lower trust: synthetic cases can be unrealistic or mislabeled, so they supplement seeds and mined cases rather than replace them. | . 📖 The flywheel reframes incidents. In a normal service a bug is fixed and forgotten. In an agent, every production failure is a free, perfectly-realistic eval case handed to you by reality — provided you have the discipline to capture it before the trace scrolls away. That discipline is the difference between an agent that gets more reliable over time and one that re-breaks the same way every quarter. 3b. The grader — three families, in descending order of trust . The grader scores one run. Pick the most trustworthy grader the task allows — and design tasks to allow the trustworthy ones. 1. Programmatic (code checks the outcome) — the gold standard. A deterministic function inspects the resulting world and returns pass/fail or a score. Did the test suite go green? Does the file contain the expected function? Is the emitted JSON valid against the schema? Did the SQL return the right rows? When you can write a programmatic grader, you almost always should: it is deterministic, free, fast, and cannot be fooled. The constraint is that not everything is mechanically checkable — but far more is than you’d think if you design the task to be checkable. “Fix the bug” is fuzzy; “fix the bug such that pytest passes” is programmatic. Engineering the task toward a programmatic grader is one of the highest-leverage moves in eval design. A common, sharp sub-form is the assertion list — a set of must and must_not predicates over the output or final state. Must contain the ticket ID; must not contain a raw API key; must leave the test suite green. Cheap to write, composable, and surprisingly expressive for “did it do the obviously-required things and avoid the obviously-forbidden ones.” . 2. LLM-as-judge (a model scores against a rubric) — for fuzzy quality at scale. When the criterion is genuinely subjective — “is this a good summary?” — you use a second model as the grader, prompted with an explicit rubric. This unlocks scale for criteria no assert can express. It is also the grader most likely to lie to you, so it comes with non-negotiable discipline: . | Calibrate against humans. A judge is worthless until you’ve checked its verdicts against human labels on a sample and measured agreement. An uncalibrated judge is a random number generator wearing a lab coat. (You’ll do this in part (e) of the exercise.) | Know the biases. Judges exhibit length bias (longer = better, regardless of substance), self-style / self-enhancement bias (prefers outputs that read like the judge’s own model would write), and position bias (in pairwise comparison, favors whichever answer came first — so swap order and average). These are documented, reproducible, and they make a judge confidently wrong. | Force it to cite evidence. Make the judge quote the specific spans that justify its verdict before it scores. This both improves accuracy and gives you something to audit — a verdict with no evidence is unfalsifiable. | Use structured output. Constrain the verdict to a typed schema (Pydantic + messages.parse) so you get a score, a reason, and cited evidence — never free-form prose you have to regex. We do exactly this below. | Prefer a strong judge. Use a frontier model (claude-opus-4-8) as judge even when the system under test is cheaper (Scout on Sonnet). Judging is often harder than doing, and a weak judge is the dominant source of eval noise. | . 3. Human (a person scores) — ground truth, used sparingly. The highest-trust grader and the least scalable. Reserve humans for two jobs: establishing the ground-truth labels you calibrate the judge against, and spot-reading transcripts to catch failures your automated graders miss (especially passing-for-the-wrong-reason). You will not human-grade your whole suite on every run; you human-grade a sample to keep the cheap graders honest. ✅ The grader heuristic. Reach for programmatic first and engineer the task to allow it. Use an LLM judge only for genuinely fuzzy quality, and only after calibrating it against humans. Keep humans in the loop as the calibration anchor, not the bulk grader. 3c. Aggregation — from noisy runs to a decision . This is where the statistics live, and where most homegrown evals quietly go wrong. Because the system is stochastic, one run of one case tells you almost nothing. You run each case k times and report rates with confidence intervals — never a single boolean. Two metrics, and the difference between them is the difference between a demo and an autonomous product: . | pass@k — “at least 1 of k runs succeeded.” Optimistic. Relevant when a human or a retry can salvage a failure: if the agent gets it right one try in three and someone picks the good one, pass@k is the metric you care about. | pass^k — “all k runs succeeded.” The reliability metric. This is what matters for autonomy: an agent that succeeds 90% of the time per step fails a 10-step task more than 60% of the time, because errors compound multiplicatively. If you are going to let the agent run unsupervised, pass^k (consistency) is your true north, and it is brutal — far harsher than pass@k, and far more honest about whether you can trust the thing alone. | . And the rule that separates signal from theater: . A change smaller than the confidence interval is noise. If your baseline is 80% ± 7% and your change measures 83%, you have learned nothing. The intervals overlap completely. Reporting “we improved 3 points” is, statistically, a lie. Either gather more samples (more cases × higher k) to shrink the interval, or accept that the change is in the noise floor and stop pretending otherwise. The width of that interval is governed by your sample size — n cases times k runs. Small suites have wide intervals and can only detect large changes; that’s a real constraint to design around, not a bug. We’ll compute these intervals with a Wilson helper in the exercise. The discipline is non-negotiable: rates with intervals, never bare booleans, and changes within the interval are noise.

136.title: 4. How evals run, operationally
136.content: The conceptual model is clean; the operational reality has a few hard parts worth naming, because this is where agent evals diverge most from running a unit suite. Isolated, reproducible fixtures — one per trial. Each run must start from an identical, pristine world and not contaminate the next run. The pattern is dead simple and robust: keep a frozen fixture directory under version control; for each trial, copy it into a fresh temp dir and run the agent there. The agent edits the copy; you grade the copy; you delete the copy. Run 2 cannot see run 1’s mutations. (You’ll see exactly this — shutil.copytree into a tempfile.mkdtemp() — in the harness below.) . Mock the side-effecting tools — let the agent think it acted. If Scout’s real toolset sends emails, charges cards, opens PRs, or posts to Slack, you cannot fire those for real across thousands of eval runs. The technique: replace side-effecting tools with mocks that record the intended action and return a plausible success, so the agent proceeds through its loop as if the action happened. You grade the recorded intent (“did it attempt to email the right person with the right content?”) rather than a real send. This is the single biggest source of the mock-vs-reality gap (Real production issues, below) — the agent passed because your mock behaved more nicely than the real world does — so keep mocks faithful and treat a passing eval over mocks as necessary, not sufficient. Parallelize — it’s embarrassingly parallel, with a cap. Cases and runs are independent: n × k trials with no data dependencies. Fan them out concurrently to turn an hour into a minute. The only constraint is a concurrency cap to respect API rate limits — a semaphore, nothing fancier. Two tiers: smoke vs full — your fast-unit-vs-slow-integration split. You cannot afford to run the deep suite on every commit (agent suites are expensive — many model calls per run, times k, times n). So you tier it, exactly the way you already tier tests: . | Smoke suite — small, cheap, k=1, a dozen core cases. Runs on every change as a fast gate. Catches gross breakage in seconds-to-minutes. | Full suite — the whole dataset, deep, k≥3 (or higher), with confidence intervals. Runs nightly and pre-release. This is the suite you gate ships on. | . Record everything: score + full transcript + op metrics. A bare score is undebuggable. For every trial, persist the complete transcript (every message, tool call, and result — this is the trace Module 09 makes first-class), the score and grader rationale, and operational metrics: tokens, latency, step count, dollar cost. When a case fails, the transcript is the only thing that tells you why; when it passes, the op metrics tell you whether it passed efficiently (an agent that takes 40 steps and $2 to do a 4-step task is failing in a way no pass/fail captures).

137.title: 5. Interpreting results — turning numbers into decisions
137.content: You have per-slice rates with intervals. Now what? Every comparison is relative. An absolute number (“76% pass”) is nearly meaningless in isolation — 76% might be triumphant or catastrophic depending on the task and your baseline. Evals earn their keep through three kinds of comparison: . | Regression gating (vs. your own baseline, in CI). Store the current production system’s scores as the baseline. On every change, re-run the suite and block the merge if any slice drops beyond its confidence interval. This is the agent-world equivalent of a red build — and the thing that makes it safe to iterate on prompts and tools at all. Per-slice, not aggregate: a 4-point drop on bugfix masked by a 4-point rise on qa nets to zero overall and ships a real regression. Gate the slices. | Model selection (run the identical suite across candidates). When a new model ships, run your unchanged suite on old and new and read the per-slice diff. This is the payoff of the whole module: it converts a model upgrade from a terrifying leap of faith into a measured, one-day A/B test. You see precisely which slices improved and which regressed, and you decide with data. “The model changed” stops being existential and becomes a diff you can read. | Trend over time. Plot scores across runs. Slow drift — from prompt rot, a dependency bump, gradual fixture decay — is invisible run-to-run and obvious over weeks. The trend line catches the slow leak. | . Validate the grader — the step everyone skips and then regrets. Your number is only as trustworthy as the thing producing it, and the grader can lie: . | Calibrate the judge against humans (the discipline from §3b), and re-calibrate when you change the rubric or the judge model. | Spot-read passing transcripts, not just failing ones. Failing transcripts get read because failures demand attention. The insidious failure is passing-for-the-wrong-reason — the agent reached the right end state by luck, by exploiting a quirk of the fixture, or by a path that won’t generalize. Your grader sees green; reality will see red. The only defense is periodically reading transcripts that passed and asking “did it pass for a reason that will hold up?” | . The decision loop, concretely. Run the suite, then: . | Within CI on every slice → ship. No slice dropped beyond its interval; the change is at worst neutral. Merge. | A slice dropped beyond its interval → read the failing transcripts. Failures cluster — a dozen failures usually share one root cause (a prompt instruction the model now over-applies, a tool returning a new error shape, a context-window overflow on big fixtures). Find the cluster, fix the root cause, re-run. | A new production failure appeared → mine it into a case. Freeze the situation as a regression case (the flywheel), confirm it now reproduces the failure, then fix it. The case is permanent insurance against re-breaking. | .

138.title: 6. End-to-end vs component evals; and online evals
138.content: So far we’ve evaluated the whole agent loop end-to-end: give it a task, let it act, grade the final world. That’s the most important kind — it measures what the user experiences. But it has a weakness: when an end-to-end eval regresses, it tells you that something broke, not what. The failure could be in retrieval, in compaction, in the judge, in a tool. Component evals localize the damage. You freeze the input to one component and test that component in isolation against a fixed expected behavior: . | Compaction (Module 04): freeze a long transcript, run your summarizer, assert the summary preserves the load-bearing facts. | Retrieval (Module 05): freeze a query set with known-relevant docs, measure recall@k and precision — no agent loop at all. | The judge itself: freeze a set of human-labeled outputs and measure judge agreement. (Yes — you eval your evaluator. The judge is a component like any other.) | . The pattern: end-to-end evals tell you the system regressed; component evals tell you which part. Run both. Component evals are cheaper, more deterministic, and they’re where a regression’s location becomes obvious. Online / production evals — the bridge to Module 09. Everything above is offline: a fixed dataset, run in CI. But production is the real distribution, and it shifts. Online evals sample live traces and grade them continuously — run an LLM judge over (a sample of) real production runs, track the pass rate as a live metric, and alarm when it dips. This is the earliest possible warning that reality has diverged from your offline suite, and it’s where evals and observability merge. We pick it up properly in Module 09; the connection to hold now is that traces are the shared substrate — the same transcript you grade offline is the trace you watch online.

139.title: 🛠️ Exercise — Build a real eval harness for Scout

140.title: Real production issues
140.content: . | Flaky, noisy evals from too-low k or an uncalibrated judge. Run k=1 and treat the boolean as truth and you’ll “improve” things that were noise and “regress” things that weren’t. The two fixes: raise k until the CI is tight enough to detect the effect you care about, and calibrate the judge so its scores mean something. Most “our evals are useless” complaints are one of these two, untreated. | Goodhart / overfitting to your own suite. Iterate against a fixed eval long enough and you tune the agent to the eval, not the task. Defenses: keep growing the suite from production (the flywheel — a moving target can’t be overfit), and hold out a slice of cases the agent is never tuned against, checked only at release. If held-out scores lag the tuned set, you’re overfitting. | The mock-vs-reality gap — passed the eval, failed in prod. Your mocked send_email returned a clean success; the real SMTP server rejected the address. Mocks that behave more nicely than reality manufacture false confidence. Keep mocks faithful to real failure modes, and treat a green offline suite as necessary, not sufficient — back it with online evals on real traces (Module 09). | Passing-for-the-wrong-reason. The agent reached the right end state by exploiting a fixture quirk, or by luck that won’t generalize. The grader sees green; production sees red. Only defense: periodically read passing transcripts, not just failing ones, and ask “would this path hold on a slightly different input?” | Judge biases lying with confidence. Length, self-style, and position biases make a judge confidently wrong — and confident wrongness is the worst kind, because it survives review. Disarm in the rubric, force evidence citation before scoring, swap order in pairwise comparisons, and re-calibrate against humans whenever you touch the judge. | Coverage gaps in the long tail. A finite suite samples the task distribution; agents fail in the unsampled tail you never wrote a case for. You can’t test your way to full coverage. Online evals on real traffic are how the tail surfaces — and each tail failure becomes a mined case, narrowing the gap over time. | Cost of big agent suites. A full agentic suite is many model calls × k × n — minutes and real dollars per run. That’s exactly why you tier: cheap smoke gate on every change, expensive full suite nightly/pre-release. Don’t run the deep suite on every commit; don’t ship on the smoke suite alone. | Model upgrades silently breaking prompts (prompt rot). The provider improves the model; your prompt, tuned to the old one, regresses on a slice or two. With no eval suite this is invisible until a user reports it. With one, the upgrade is a one-day measured A/B — you read the per-slice diff and decide. This is the single most important thing evals buy you: they turn “the model changed” from existential risk into a diff you can read. | The temptation to skip evals because they’re unglamorous. No one demos an eval harness. It ships no user-facing feature. So under deadline it’s the first thing cut — and the teams that cut it ship agents that fail silently and degrade invisibly, because they have no instrument pointed at quality. The teams that ship reliable agents treat eval engineering as first-class, resourced comparably to product work, owned not delegated. Eval development is roughly as much effort as product development. That sounds expensive until you price the alternative: shipping a stochastic system into production with no way to know if it works. The eval suite is the product’s quality, made measurable. Build it first-class or build it never. | .

141.title: Check yourself
141.content: . | Name the four reasons you cannot unit-test an agent, and for each, the unit-test assumption it violates. | What is the difference between an eval and a benchmark? Which one gates your ship, and why can’t a benchmark do that job? | Why is pass^k the metric that matters for autonomy, and pass@k the one that matters when a human is in the loop? Work out the 10-step example. | Your baseline slice is 80% ± 7%; your change measures 84%. Ship or not? What single change to your methodology would let you tell? | Order the three grader families by trust. Give a fuzzy task and rewrite it so a programmatic grader becomes possible. | What is “passing-for-the-wrong-reason,” why do failing-only reviews miss it, and what’s the one practice that catches it? | Explain why mocking side-effecting tools is necessary, and the specific gap it introduces. How do you guard against that gap? | A new model ships. Walk through, step by step, how your harness turns the upgrade from a gamble into a one-day decision. | Why is your private eval suite a moat, and what daily discipline keeps it growing? | .

142.title: Further reading
142.content: . | Anthropic — “Building effective agents” and the applied-AI engineering posts: evals as the backbone of agent reliability; the smoke-vs-full and online-eval patterns. | Anthropic Cookbook — evaluations & LLM-as-judge recipes: end-to-end judge construction, rubric design, and calibration in code. | “Judging LLM-as-a-Judge” (Zheng et al., MT-Bench / Chatbot Arena): the canonical study of judge biases (length, position, self-enhancement) and how to measure judge–human agreement. | SWE-bench / τ-bench papers: how agentic benchmarks are constructed and graded — and, read critically, the contamination and construct-validity caveats. | Wilson score interval (Wilson, 1927) and bootstrap confidence intervals: the statistics behind “changes smaller than the CI are noise.” For most eval work the Wilson helper above is enough. | Eval platforms — Braintrust, Langfuse: when your from-scratch harness outgrows scripts, these add datasets, run storage, judge orchestration, and dashboards. Learn the from-scratch harness first — the platform is a convenience over the concepts you just built, not a substitute for understanding them. | . → Next: Module 09 — Observability, Tracing & Debugging .

144.title: Module 09 — Observability, Tracing & Debugging
144.content: You already know distributed tracing. You know what a span is, you know context propagation, you know how to read a flame graph and spot the slow downstream call. This module is not going to re-teach any of that. It’s going to show you what’s different when the thing you’re instrumenting is an agent — and why the observability stack you’d reach for on a normal service is necessary but nowhere near sufficient. Here’s the thesis up front, because the rest of the module hangs off it: an agent’s behavior is a causal chain, and the interesting failures live in the relationship between steps, not inside any single step. A microservice request fails because this span returned a 500. An agent run fails because the model misread a tool result five steps ago, formed a wrong belief, and then executed flawlessly on that wrong belief for the next twelve steps. Every individual span is status: ok. The trace is a disaster. Your normal logs — request in, response out, latency, error rate — will show you a clean, successful, expensive run that produced garbage. You will not be able to debug it, cost-control it, or improve it, because you cannot see it. Teams that ship good harnesses instrument them like high-traffic production services, because that’s what they are: nondeterministic, multi-step, expensive, and failure-prone in ways that don’t surface as exceptions. You cannot improve what you can’t see. For agents, “seeing” means capturing the full session as a replayable causal chain.

145.title: Learning objectives
145.content: By the end of this module you will be able to: . | Articulate why agents need first-class observability more than ordinary services, and why call-level LLM monitoring is not agent observability. | Map the trace/span data model onto an agent run, and name what each span must carry that a normal RPC span does not. | Build a from-scratch trace logger (decorator + context manager) that writes per-run JSONL, and a tree-printer + summary over it. | Instrument Scout’s loop with Langfuse, and place LangSmith and Braintrust correctly in the landscape. | Debug a multi-step failure by finding where the chain went wrong (usually far upstream of the symptom) and replaying it deterministically. | Wire production trace sampling into online evals — closing the loop back to Module 8. | .

146.title: Why agents need this more than normal services
146.content: Four properties of agents each break a load-bearing assumption of conventional observability. Nondeterminism. The same input produces different trajectories. A bug that appears one run in twenty is not reproducible by re-running — the model just does something else. Without a recording of exactly what happened, the bug is gone. (This is why replay, below, is not a nice-to-have.) . Multi-step causality. A single user request fans out into 5, 20, 80 model calls and tool calls. The failure is rarely in the step that threw. It’s a belief the model formed early and carried forward. Your trace has to preserve the whole chain so you can walk backward from symptom to cause. Cost. Every step burns tokens, and tokens are money and latency. A run that silently takes 40 steps instead of 8 costs 5x and you’ll never notice from a latency dashboard that says “p95: 45s, within SLO.” You need per-step token accounting to see it. (Module 10 is where you fix cost; here you measure it.) . Invisible failure. The worst one. The agent returns a confident, well-formed answer that is wrong. HTTP 200. No exception. No log line that says “I made this up.” In production agent fleets it’s common for a meaningful fraction of tasks to fail this way — silently, looking exactly like success. Your error-rate dashboard reads 0.1% while the real task-failure rate is 18%. The only way to see the gap is to capture full traces and grade their content, not their status codes. ✅ Checkpoint. If your mental model is “agent observability = log the prompt and completion and track token spend,” you have LLM monitoring, not agent observability. The difference is the full-session causal chain. Hold that distinction — everything below builds on it.

147.title: The data model: traces and spans, agent-flavored
147.content: Lean on what you know. A trace is one full agent run — one session, one user request driven to completion. A span is a nested step within it: each model call, each tool call, each sub-agent invocation, each retrieval. Spans nest exactly the way you’d expect — a sub-agent span contains the model and tool spans of that sub-agent’s own loop. A trace ID threads the whole thing; span IDs and parent-span IDs give you the tree. None of this is new. What’s new is two things. The payload is huge, semi-structured text. A normal span carries http.method=GET, http.status=200, db.rows=42 — small, structured, cheap. An agent span carries the full rendered prompt (which can be tens of thousands of tokens), the full completion, the tool arguments, the tool result (which might be a 5,000-line file the model just read). The “attributes” on an agent span are prompts and completions and tool I/O. This changes everything downstream — storage cost, query patterns, PII exposure, redaction needs (more in Real production issues). The interesting failure is semantic and lives between spans. On a microservice, you find the bad span by its status code and you’re basically done. On an agent, every span succeeded. The failure is: span 7 was a read_file that returned an old version of the config; span 8’s model call read it correctly but the file was stale; spans 9 through 20 confidently built on a wrong fact. No span is red. The bug is the relationship between span 7’s output and span 20’s behavior. You find it by reading the transcript as a narrative, not by filtering for errors. The consequence: capture the full session, not just call-level metrics. A dashboard of “mean tokens per call” and “tool call p99 latency” is useful but it is aggregate. To debug a specific bad run you need that run’s complete, ordered, nested trace with every payload intact. Aggregates tell you that something is wrong; the full trace tells you what. 📖 OpenTelemetry note. OTel has emerging GenAI semantic conventions — standardized span names (gen_ai.completion), attributes (gen_ai.usage.input_tokens, gen_ai.request.model), and event shapes for LLM and agent operations. They’re still stabilizing in mid-2026, but they matter: they’re the interop substrate that lets you emit one trace and view it in any OTel-compatible backend. Treat them as the standard you instrument toward, even when you’re using a vendor SDK that wraps them. We’ll come back to lock-in vs. portability at the end. What every span must carry . Per-span, capture: . | Full prompt + completion (or a reference/hash if you’re storing payloads out-of-band for size or PII reasons). | Tool name, arguments, and result for tool spans. | Token counts — input, output, cache_read, cache_creation — straight off resp.usage. This is the raw material for cost. | Latency (you already do this). | Model and params — model ID, effort, max_tokens, whatever shapes the call. | stop_reason — end_turn, tool_use, max_tokens, refusal. A run that ends on max_tokens truncated mid-thought; a run that ends on refusal was declined. These are first-class signals, not footnotes. | Errors — tool failures, API errors, denials from the permission gate. | The trace/session ID threading it all. | . Per-run (aggregate the spans), compute: . | Steps per task — the single best health metric. A task that used to take 8 steps now takes 30: something regressed. | Tool-error rate — per tool. The insight you will never get from anecdote: “the search tool has a 30% error rate” is invisible one run at a time and screaming at you across a thousand traces. | Cache-hit rate — cache_read / (input + cache_read). Drops silently when someone interpolates a timestamp into the system prompt (Module 4’s silent invalidators). | Compaction frequency — how often you’re hitting the context ceiling. | Total tokens and cost. | Success — from an eval or a label, not from stop_reason. (The whole point: success is semantic.) | .

148.title: 🛠️ Build it from scratch first
148.content:
Before reaching for a platform, build the data model by hand. It’s ~60 lines, it makes the abstraction concrete, and — genuinely — a JSONL-per-run tracer is a legitimate production tool. You’ll understand exactly what Langfuse is doing for you when you adopt it, instead of treating it as magic. We’re instrumenting Scout’s loop from Module 3. Recall its shape: a while loop calling client.messages.create(...), dispatching tool_use blocks through a permission gate, feeding tool_result blocks back. We want a span for every model call and every tool call, all sharing one trace ID, written to one file per run. The tracer . # scout/tracing.py import json, time, uuid, contextvars from contextlib import contextmanager from dataclasses import dataclass, field, asdict from pathlib import Path # The current trace travels implicitly via a contextvar, so the model-call and # tool-call wrappers don't have to thread a `trace` argument through every layer. _current_trace: contextvars.ContextVar = contextvars.ContextVar("trace", default=None) @dataclass class Span: name: str span_type: str # "model" | "tool" | "agent" span_id: str = field(default_factory=lambda: uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]) parent_id: str | None = None start: float = 0.0 end: float = 0.0 input: dict = field(default_factory=dict) output: dict = field(default_factory=dict) tokens: dict = field(default_factory=dict) # input/output/cache_read/cache_creation cost_usd: float = 0.0 error: str | None = None @property def latency_ms(self) -> float: return round((self.end - self.start) * 1000, 1) class Trace: def __init__(self, name: str, log_dir: str = "traces"): self.trace_id = uuid.uuid4().hex[:12] self.name = name self.spans: list[Span] = [] self._stack: list[str] = [] # parent span ids, for nesting Path(log_dir).mkdir(exist_ok=True) self.path = Path(log_dir) / f"{self.name}-{self.trace_id}.jsonl" def flush(self): with self.path.open("w") as f: f.write(json.dumps({"trace_id": self.trace_id, "name": self.name}) + "
") for s in self.spans: f.write(json.dumps({**asdict(s), "latency_ms": s.latency_ms}) + "
") @contextmanager def trace_run(name: str): tr = Trace(name) token = _current_trace.set(tr) try: yield tr finally: tr.flush() _current_trace.reset(token) @contextmanager def span(name: str, span_type: str): tr = _current_trace.get() if tr is None: # tracing disabled — no-op yield None return s = Span(name=name, span_type=span_type, parent_id=tr._stack[-1] if tr._stack else None, start=time.time()) tr.spans.append(s) tr._stack.append(s.span_id) try: yield s except Exception as e: s.error = repr(e) raise finally: s.end = time.time() tr._stack.pop() . Two design notes worth pausing on. The contextvar is doing the same job OTel’s context propagation does — making the active trace ambient so deep call sites don’t have to pass it explicitly. And the _stack is what gives you nesting: a tool span opened inside a model span gets the model span as its parent, so sub-agent trees fall out naturally. Pricing helper . # Opus 4.8: $5 / $25 per 1M in/out; cache reads ~0.1x input, writes ~1.25x. PRICES = {"claude-opus-4-8": (5.0, 25.0)} def cost_of(model: str, usage) -> float: pin, pout = PRICES.get(model, (0.0, 0.0)) return round( (usage.input_tokens / 1e6) * pin + (usage.output_tokens / 1e6) * pout + (getattr(usage, "cache_read_input_tokens", 0) / 1e6) * pin * 0.1 + (getattr(usage, "cache_creation_input_tokens", 0) / 1e6) * pin * 1.25, 6, ) . Wiring it into the loop . The instrumentation is two wrappers. Around the model call: . def call_model(client, messages, system, tools): with span("model_call", "model") as s: resp = client.messages.create( model="claude-opus-4-8", max_tokens=4096, system=system, tools=tools, messages=messages, ) if s is not None: s.input = {"messages": messages[-1:], "n_messages": len(messages)} # last turn + depth s.output = {"stop_reason": resp.stop_reason, "content": [b.model_dump() for b in resp.content]} u = resp.usage s.tokens = {"input": u.input_tokens, "output": u.output_tokens, "cache_read": getattr(u, "cache_read_input_tokens", 0), "cache_creation": getattr(u, "cache_creation_input_tokens", 0)} s.cost_usd = cost_of("claude-opus-4-8", u) return resp . And around each tool dispatch (Scout’s dispatch from Module 3): . def dispatch(tool_use_block, gate): with span(f"tool:{tool_use_block.name}", "tool") as s: if s is not None: s.input = {"args": tool_use_block.input} result = run_tool_with_gate(tool_use_block, gate) # your Module 3 logic if s is not None: s.output = {"is_error": result.get("is_error", False), "content": result["content"][:2000]} # truncate huge results return result . Then the top-level call site opens the trace: . with trace_run("scout-session"): run_scout_loop(user_prompt) # everything inside is now traced . Notice what we captured per model span: last message + history depth (full prompt is recoverable but huge), the content blocks of the response (so we keep tool_use blocks, not just text), stop_reason, all four token counts, and cost. That’s the full per-span checklist from above. And note we truncate tool results to 2,000 chars in the output view — the trade-off between storing everything (replayable but expensive) and storing enough to debug. For real replay you’d store the untruncated result keyed by span ID; here we keep it simple. Reading the trace: tree + summary . A JSONL file is not a debugging tool until you can read it as a narrative. The pretty-printer turns the flat span list back into the nested tree, and the summary computes the per-run metrics: . # scout/trace_view.py import json, sys from collections import defaultdict def load(path): with open(path) as f: lines = [json.loads(l) for l in f] return lines[0], lines[1:] # header, spans def print_tree(spans): children = defaultdict(list) roots = [] for s in spans: (children[s["parent_id"]].append(s) if s["parent_id"] else roots.append(s)) def walk(s, depth): tok = s["tokens"].get("output", 0) if s["tokens"] else 0 err = " ERROR" if s["error"] else "" extra = (f" stop={s['output'].get('stop_reason')}" if s["span_type"] == "model" else "") print(f"{' '*depth}{s['name']:<28} {s['latency_ms']:>7}ms " f"{tok:>5}tok ${s['cost_usd']:.4f}{extra}{err}") for c in children[s["span_id"]]: walk(c, depth + 1) for r in roots: walk(r, 0) def summary(spans): model = [s for s in spans if s["span_type"] == "model"] tools = [s for s in spans if s["span_type"] == "tool"] tool_errs = sum(1 for s in tools if s["output"].get("is_error")) tok = lambda k: sum((s["tokens"] or {}).get(k, 0) for s in model) print("
--- run summary ---") print(f"model calls (steps): {len(model)}") print(f"tool calls: {len(tools)} errors: {tool_errs} " f"({100*tool_errs/max(len(tools),1):.0f}%)") print(f"tokens in/out: {tok('input')} / {tok('output')}") print(f"cache hit rate: " f"{100*tok('cache_read')/max(tok('input')+tok('cache_read'),1):.0f}%") print(f"total cost: ${sum(s['cost_usd'] for s in model):.4f}") if __name__ == "__main__": _, spans = load(sys.argv[1]) print_tree(spans) summary(spans) . Run it and you get the run as a tree — every model call, every nested tool call, latency and tokens and cost on each line, stop_reason on model calls, ERROR flags where things failed — followed by the summary block. That summary line “tool calls: 14 errors: 4 (29%)” is the “tool X has a 30% error rate” insight, made visible. You built it. ✅ Checkpoint. You now have, in ~120 lines, the core of every agent observability platform: nested spans, per-span token/cost capture, a tree view, and run-level aggregates. Everything a vendor adds is operational scale on top of this model — a database, a UI, search, multi-run analytics, retention. Worth understanding what you’re paying for.

149.title: Swap in Langfuse
149.content: For a single dev loop, JSONL files are great. For a fleet — thousands of runs a day, multiple engineers, “show me every run last week where the search tool errored” — you want a backend with a database and a UI. Langfuse is the open-source baseline here: self-hostable (so it’s data-residency friendly — your prompts and completions never leave your infra), and as of January 2026 it’s backed by ClickHouse, which acquired it — a signal that the storage layer underneath is built for the high-cardinality, high-volume trace workloads agents generate. Two ways to instrument. The decorator is the fastest: . from langfuse import observe, get_client langfuse = get_client() @observe() # this function becomes a span def dispatch(tool_use_block, gate): result = run_tool_with_gate(tool_use_block, gate) langfuse.update_current_span( input={"tool": tool_use_block.name, "args": tool_use_block.input}, output={"is_error": result.get("is_error", False)}, ) return result @observe() def run_scout_loop(user_prompt): # the whole run becomes the trace ... Any @observe()-decorated function called inside another becomes a child span — the nesting you built by hand with _stack, done by the decorator via the same kind of context propagation. For the model call specifically, Langfuse ships an Anthropic wrapper that auto-captures the request, response, model, and — critically — usage, so you get token counts and cost without writing the cost_of plumbing: . from langfuse.anthropic import Anthropic # drop-in for anthropic.Anthropic client = Anthropic() # Every client.messages.create(...) inside an @observe() context is now a span # with prompt, completion, model, stop_reason, and token usage captured. resp = client.messages.create( model="claude-opus-4-8", max_tokens=4096, system=system, tools=tools, messages=messages, ) . If you need finer control than the decorator gives — custom span boundaries, manual nesting — there’s langfuse.start_as_current_span(...) as a context manager, which is the direct analog of your hand-built span(). Set a stable session_id per Scout run and every span lands under one trace in the UI, where you get the tree view, token/cost rollups, latency breakdowns, and search across runs — the same data model you built, operationalized. 📖 The alternatives, placed correctly. | LangSmith — best when your stack is LangChain / LangGraph. The tracing is deeply native to those frameworks; spans map onto chains, agents, and graph nodes with near-zero instrumentation. If you’re not on LangChain, its advantage mostly evaporates. | Braintrust — eval-first. Its center of gravity is treating evals as CI gates: you wire trace-derived test cases into a suite that blocks a deploy on regression. Generous free tier. Reach for it when your discipline is “no agent change ships without passing the eval gate” (the Module 8 mindset, productized). | . Which one? Default to Langfuse if you want open-source, self-hosting, or data residency — it’s the safe baseline and the data model is the one you just learned. Choose LangSmith if you live in LangChain/LangGraph. Choose Braintrust if eval-gated CI is the workflow you’re building around. And whichever you pick, prefer the OTel GenAI conventions underneath so the trace outlives the vendor.

150.title: Debugging multi-step failures
150.content: This is the part your microservice instincts mislead you on, so go slow. The workflow: . | Capture the full trace. You can’t debug what you didn’t record — and because of nondeterminism, you can’t reliably reproduce it by re-running. The trace is the evidence. | Find where the chain went wrong. The symptom — wrong final answer, infinite loop, blown budget — appears at the end. The cause is almost always upstream. Read the transcript forward as a narrative and find the first span where the model’s belief diverged from reality. That’s your bug. It is rarely the span that looks broken. | Form a hypothesis. “At span 7 the model read a stale config and believed the flag was off; everything after is correct reasoning on a wrong premise.” | Replay. Re-run the loop logic against the recorded model responses to confirm the hypothesis deterministically. | . Step 4 is the superpower, so let’s build it. Replay . The idea: record every (request, response) pair from the model during a run. Then re-run your loop with the model mocked — instead of calling the API, you replay the recorded responses in order. Now your loop logic runs deterministically against the exact trajectory that failed. You can add logging, set breakpoints, fix a dispatch bug, and re-run as many times as you want, and it’s the same run every time. The nondeterminism is frozen. # scout/replay.py import json from pathlib import Path class Recorder: """Wrap the client; record every model response to a file.""" def __init__(self, client, path): self._client = client self._path = Path(path) self._records = [] def create(self, **kwargs): resp = self._client.messages.create(**kwargs) self._records.append(resp.model_dump()) # full response, serializable return resp def save(self): self._path.write_text(json.dumps(self._records)) class Player: """Replay recorded responses in order. No network, fully deterministic.""" def __init__(self, path): self._records = json.loads(Path(path).read_text()) self._i = 0 def create(self, **kwargs): from anthropic.types import Message rec = self._records[self._i] self._i += 1 return Message.model_validate(rec) # reconstruct the SDK object . Record on a live run, replay forever after: . # Record: rec = Recorder(anthropic.Anthropic(), "fail-run.json") run_scout_loop(prompt, client=rec); rec.save() # Replay against your loop logic, no API calls, deterministic: run_scout_loop(prompt, client=Player("fail-run.json")) . Because Player.create reconstructs the real SDK Message object, your loop’s resp.stop_reason, resp.content, resp.usage all work unchanged — the loop can’t tell it’s talking to a recording. Now the failing run reproduces on demand. You step through it, you find that span 7 returned a stale read, you fix the staleness check, and you replay to confirm the chain now goes right. That is how you debug nondeterministic systems: you make them deterministic. 📖 And this is how you build taste. Reading transcripts — not metrics, the actual prompt/completion/tool-IO narrative of real runs — is the single highest-leverage habit in agent engineering. It’s the same skill Module 8 leaned on for writing evals: you cannot write a good judge or a good unit eval for a failure mode you’ve never seen in a real transcript. Replay and transcript-reading are two sides of one practice. Common failure signatures in a trace . Once you’ve read a few hundred traces, the shapes become recognizable: . | Context starvation — the model is reasoning without a fact it needs, because compaction (Module 4) dropped it or it was never retrieved. In the trace: a model span whose input is missing something an earlier span produced. Often co-occurs with a compaction span just upstream. | A bad tool result the model trusted — a tool returned wrong/stale/empty data, the model took it at face value, everything downstream is built on it. The tool span looks is_error: false (it didn’t crash, it just lied). The classic upstream-cause bug. | Tool-arg hallucination — the model calls a tool with an argument it invented (a file path that doesn’t exist, an ID it made up). In the trace: a tool span whose input doesn’t correspond to anything any prior span surfaced, usually followed by an error result and a confused recovery. | Infinite loop — the same tool span with the same args repeating. Trivially obvious in the tree, invisible in a latency metric until the run blows its budget. (Your steps-per-task metric catches this in aggregate.) | Sub-agent solved the wrong problem — a sub-agent span tree that’s internally coherent and successful but answers a question the parent didn’t ask, because the delegated instruction was ambiguous. You have to open the child trace to see it; the parent just sees a plausible result come back. | .

151.title: Online evals: closing the loop to Module 8
151.content: Observability and evals are two sides of the same coin. Traces are the substrate evals run on, and production failures become new eval cases. Module 8 built the eval methodology; this is where it meets production. The pattern is continuous: sample live traces, run a grader on each, alert on drift. Three layers stack here: . | Unit evals on discrete steps — programmatic, cheap, run on every (or sampled) trace. “Did the write_file span ever write outside the project root?” “Did any tool span exceed 3 retries?” | LLM-as-judge regression suites — the Module 8 judge, run against sampled production traces, scoring final-answer quality on traces where you have no ground-truth label. This is how you measure the real task-failure rate — the 18% that stop_reason hides. | Continuous production sampling for drift — grade, say, 2% of all traces on a rolling basis, track the score over time, and alert when it drifts down. A model update, a prompt change, a tool that started returning a new error shape — drift catches regressions your CI evals didn’t anticipate. | . def online_eval(trace_path, sample_rate=0.02): import random if random.random() > sample_rate: return _, spans = load(trace_path) final = next(s for s in reversed(spans) if s["span_type"] == "model" and not s["output"].get("stop_reason") == "tool_use") score = llm_judge(final["output"]["content"]) # your Module 8 judge log_score(trace_path, score) # to Langfuse, a metrics sink, etc. if score < THRESHOLD: flag_for_review(trace_path) # ← becomes a new eval case . That last line is the flywheel. A low-scoring production trace gets flagged, a human looks at it, and if it’s a real failure it becomes a permanent regression case in your Module 8 suite. Observability feeds evals; evals catch regressions; caught regressions harden the suite. The trace you captured to debug today is the eval case that prevents the same failure tomorrow.

152.title: Real production issues
152.content: . | The 18%-fail-silently problem. Worth restating because it’s the whole reason this module exists: a large fraction of agent task failures produce HTTP 200, no exception, no error log — a confident wrong answer. Your ops dashboards are blind to it by construction. Only content-level grading of sampled traces surfaces it. If you take one thing from this module: error rate is not failure rate. | PII and cost in captured prompts. You are now logging full prompts and completions — which means full user data, possibly PII, possibly secrets the user pasted. This is a security surface (Module 11): you need redaction at capture time, sampling to limit volume, and a retention policy. “We log every prompt forever” is a breach waiting to happen and a compliance problem in regulated domains. Redact before it hits storage, not after. | Trace volume and cost at scale. Agent traces are big (huge text payloads) and numerous (many spans per run). Storing 100% of full payloads for a high-traffic fleet gets expensive fast. Sampling strategies: keep 100% of metadata (cheap, enables aggregates and the steps/error/cost metrics) but sample full payloads — and bias the sample toward the interesting tail (always keep failed runs, runs over a step threshold, runs that hit refusal or max_tokens). Head-based random sampling throws away exactly the failures you most need. | Symptom far from cause. Internalize that the red span is rarely the bug. The discipline is reading backward from symptom to the first divergence, not jumping to the span that threw. New engineers waste days “fixing” the downstream span that was correctly processing upstream garbage. | Nondeterminism makes bugs non-reproducible — without replay. “Works on the rerun” is not a fix; it’s the bug hiding. Record-and-replay is the only reliable way to reproduce, and you should build it into the harness early, not bolt it on during an incident. | Vendor lock-in vs. OTel portability. Vendor SDKs are convenient and their auto-instrumentation saves real work. The risk is that your traces become a proprietary asset you can’t move. Mitigate by instrumenting toward the OTel GenAI conventions — emit standard spans and attributes, let the vendor consume them. Then switching backends is a config change, not a re-instrumentation project. | Instrumenting through framework abstraction layers. If you’re on a framework (Module 7), the loop is inside the library — you don’t own the call site where you’d drop a span. This is exactly why the framework-native integrations (LangSmith for LangChain, Langfuse’s callback handlers) exist: they hook the framework’s internals. The flip side, and the Module 7 warning made concrete: when the framework owns the loop, your observability is only as good as its instrumentation hooks. If it doesn’t surface a span boundary you need, you can’t add one. Evaluate that before you adopt. | Observability is the prerequisite for everything downstream. You cannot do cost control (Module 10) without per-step token accounting. You cannot detect drift without continuous trace grading. The industry framing — that something like 40% of enterprise AI failures will trace to inadequate eval and monitoring rather than to model capability — is a way of saying: the model is usually good enough; the failure is that nobody could see what it was doing. Instrumentation is not the polish you add at the end. It’s the foundation the rest of the production stack stands on. | .

153.title: Check yourself
153.content: . | Your error-rate dashboard shows 0.2% over the last day, but users are complaining the agent “gets things wrong a lot.” Both can be true. Explain how, and what you’d instrument to measure the real number. | Why does re-running a failed agent task usually fail to reproduce the bug, and how does record-and-replay solve it? What exactly are you mocking? | A run produces a wrong final answer at span 40. You read the trace. Where do you start looking, and why is span 40 almost certainly not where the bug is? | Name three things an agent model span must carry that a normal RPC span does not, and say what each one lets you compute or debug. | You’re storing full traces for a fleet doing 500K runs/day and the bill is alarming. Describe a sampling strategy that cuts cost without blinding you to failures. | Explain the flywheel between observability and evals (Module 8) in two sentences. What’s the artifact that flows from one to the other? | You picked a vendor for tracing. What’s the one architectural choice that keeps you from being locked in, and why does it matter? | .
