The agent handed broad OAuth scopes or prod creds “to be safe” has a blast radius equal to its permissions, not its task. One injection then equals full account/system compromise. Narrow the grant to the task. | Supply chain — MCP servers, community skills, tools you didn’t audit. An MCP server or installed skill runs with your agent’s trust and sees its tool I/O. A malicious or compromised one is a backdoor inside your trust boundary. Audit and pin third-party agent components exactly as you’d vet a dependency — more so, because they execute against your data. | Data exfiltration via tool calls. Exfil doesn’t need curl. A tool that fetches an image URL, posts to a webhook, or even writes to a shared doc can smuggle data out by encoding it into an argument. Audit every outward-facing tool as an exfiltration vector. | Secrets leaking into logs and traces (Module 9 overlap). You now log full prompts, completions, and tool I/O. Without capture-time redaction, that store is your PII/secret breach. Redact before storage; set retention. | The impossibility of a perfect model-layer defense. Internalize that no system prompt and no fine-tune robustly stops injection. This is why the answers are containment + HITL + least privilege. Anyone selling a model-layer silver bullet is selling something. | Outward-facing irreversible mistakes in regulated domains. The recruiting agent that emails real candidates, the finance agent that moves real money, the health agent that edits a real record — wrong here is a liability event, not a bug. HITL on the irreversible step is mandatory, and the audit trail is how you answer for it. | Red-teaming as ongoing practice. Adversarial evals are not a launch checklist item you tick once. The model drifts under you and attackers iterate, so the security suite runs forever, as a regression gate, on every model bump and every new tool. | .

192.title: Check yourself
192.content: . | Why is there no “parameterized query” fix for prompt injection? What property of LLMs makes the data/instruction boundary uncloseable at the model layer? | Name the three legs of the lethal trifecta. For a code-execution agent, which single control is cheapest to remove a leg, and which leg does it remove? | Your permission policy auto-allows ls but prompts on send_email. State the organizing principle in one sentence — and explain why auto-allowing read-only commands improves security rather than weakening it. | A teammate proposes a “security” system prompt as the primary injection defense. What’s your objection, and what do you propose instead? | The sandbox runs with --network none. Which OWASP Agentic risk does that directly mitigate, and which does it do nothing for? | Why must outward-facing/irreversible actions never get a session-wide “always allow”? | Where do security and observability (Module 9) overlap, and why is redaction a security control? | .

193.title: Further reading
193.content: . | OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, and the Top 10 for Agentic Applications (2026) — the canonical threat catalogs. | Simon Willison, “The lethal trifecta” and his ongoing prompt-injection writing — the clearest mental models in the field. | Anthropic docs: code-execution / sandboxing containers, the system & operator message channels and <system-reminder> provenance, and the memory tool (and the cautions on trusting its contents). | Your own host’s threat tolerance: Docker vs gVisor vs Firecracker/microVMs — read on the shared-kernel risk before you decide Docker is enough for genuinely hostile code. | . → Next: Module 11B — The Human Interface: Steering, Escalation & Trust .

195.title: Module 11B — The Human Interface: Steering, Escalation & Trust
195.content: Module 11 was about keeping the agent inside the fence — guardrails, sandboxing, the permission gate, human-in-the-loop as a security control. This module is about the other half of the same problem: an agent you cannot make perfectly reliable still has to be useful, and the only way it becomes useful is if a human is willing to hand it real work. That willingness is not a function of the model’s benchmark scores. It is a function of how the human and the agent talk to each other. Here is the thesis, stated plainly and meant to be taken literally: for agents, the human-agent interface is the mechanism by which you manage the risk of mistakes and earn the trust to grant autonomy. UX is not the polish you add at the end. It is the load-bearing trust-and-control layer. The gap between an impressive demo and “I’ll let it touch production / talk to real customers / move money” is overwhelmingly interaction design and recoverability, not raw capability. And the sharp version of the claim, the one worth internalizing: the reliability problem and the UX problem are two sides of the same coin. A perfectly reliable agent would need no steering, no escalation, no legibility surface, no undo — you’d fire it and forget it. Because no such agent exists, every gap in reliability has to be covered by an affordance at the human boundary. The interface is where you spend whatever reliability you couldn’t build. Designing that interface is engineering, not decoration, and it’s what this module teaches. This is deliberately a module about the design and engineering of the human/agent boundary — not about visual design, color, or layout. Every surface here is something you build into Scout’s loop.

196.title: Learning objectives
196.content: By the end you will be able to: . | Articulate why the human interface is a risk-management and trust mechanism, not a cosmetic layer, and connect it to the reliability problem. | Implement steering of a running agent: streaming output, cancellable tool execution, and queuing/injecting user messages at loop boundaries — without killing the run. | Treat escalation as a first-class design surface: design “ask” into the toolset and calibrate ask-rate by reversibility, blast radius, and confidence. | Build a legibility surface that lets a human understand a multi-hour run in seconds, and use it as a cheap drift-detector. | Reason about inspecting and correcting a live run — why true mid-run correction is a frontier problem, and why append-an-event is the clean approach (and how it collides with prompt caching’s append-only invariant). | Deepen the approval/confirmation gate into a real product surface: previews, blast-radius rendering, “always allow,” batching, plan mode, and graduated autonomy levels. | Recognize the production failure modes — the demo-to-trust gap, ask-rate miscalibration, illegible long runs, over-automation — and design against them. | .

197.title: 1. Why the interface is the trust layer
197.content: Start from a fact you already accepted in Modules 08–11: agents fail. They hallucinate tool arguments, misread state, pursue the wrong sub-goal, and drift over long runs. You mitigate with evals, observability, guardrails — but you never reach zero. The residual risk is permanent. A reliable system you can’t fully trust is useless; a trustworthy interface around an unreliable system is deployable. The difference is entirely in the affordances at the boundary: . | If stopping the agent is one keystroke and instantly safe, a user will let it run on far riskier tasks than if stopping means killing a process and cleaning up a half-finished mess. | If every action shows a preview and a diff before it commits, a user will grant write access they’d never grant to an opaque black box. | If a mistake is one git revert away, the user’s downside is bounded, so they tolerate more autonomy. | . None of those properties live in the model. They live in the harness — in the interface you build. This is why two products on the identical model can have wildly different adoption: the one with better steering, clearer approvals, and cheaper recovery gets trusted with real work, and the other stays a demo. That is the whole game. Autonomy granted is a function of how cheap inspection is and how survivable mistakes are. Every section below is one lever on that function. 📖 Reading: Re-skim Module 11’s reversibility criterion for gating — it returns here as the calibration axis for escalation. Re-skim Module 03’s agent loop and permission gate; everything here hangs off them.

198.title: 2. Steering a running agent
198.content: Classic chat is request/response: you send, the model answers, done. Agents break that model. A Scout run is not a turn — it’s a trajectory that can last minutes to hours across many tool calls. During that time the user is not absent; they’re watching, and they need to be able to interrupt, redirect, or answer a question mid-flight, without killing the run. That requires four engineering primitives. These are not exotic — every serious agent platform exposes exactly them, which is the tell that they’re the real load-bearing set: . | Streaming output, token-by-token, while tools run. Use client.messages.stream(...) and surface text_stream as it arrives. Streaming is not a latency nicety here — it’s the observability channel for the human steerer. A silent agent is an un-steerable agent; you can only redirect what you can see. | Cancellable / interruptible tool execution. When the user hits interrupt mid-bash, what happens to the half-finished command? You need a policy: kill the subprocess, mark the tool result as interrupted, and feed that back to the model so it knows the action didn’t complete. The agent’s belief and reality must stay consistent. | Queuing user messages typed mid-turn, injected at the next loop boundary. The user types “actually, focus on the backend” while the agent is three tool calls deep. You don’t splice it into the current turn — you enqueue it and inject it as a new message at the next loop boundary, where the message list is in a clean, consistent state. | A permission / confirmation gate (Modules 03/11) — the synchronous pause point. Deepened in §6. | . Why is instant, safe interruption so disproportionately load-bearing? Because it inverts the user’s risk calculus. If stopping is one keystroke and reversible, the cost of letting the agent try something is small — worst case you stop it and undo. People grant far more autonomy when the exit is cheap. The interrupt button is, paradoxically, the feature that lets you remove yourself from the loop. This connects forward to Module 12: streaming and interruptibility are exactly what durable execution makes robust. A run that can suspend/resume can also pause cleanly for a human and pick up where it left off. Scout’s loop, made steerable . Scout’s loop (Module 03) is roughly: build messages → call the model → if tool calls, execute them → append results → repeat. The steering version threads a queue and an interrupt flag through it: . import queue, threading class Steerable: """Steering state shared between the UI thread and the agent loop.""" def __init__(self): self.inbox = queue.Queue() # user messages typed mid-run self.interrupt = threading.Event() def submit(self, text: str): # called from the UI / input thread self.inbox.put(text) def stop(self): # the one-keystroke interrupt self.interrupt.set() def drain(steer: Steerable) -> list[dict]: """Pull any queued user messages; called at loop boundaries only.""" msgs = [] while not steer.inbox.empty(): msgs.append({"role": "user", "content": steer.inbox.get()}) return msgs def run_loop(client, messages, tools, steer: Steerable): while True: # --- inject queued steering at the boundary, never mid-turn --- messages += drain(steer) # --- stream the assistant turn so the human can see + react --- with client.messages.stream( model="claude-opus-4-8", max_tokens=16000, tools=tools, messages=messages, ) as stream: for text in stream.text_stream: render(text) # the steering observability channel if steer.interrupt.is_set(): stream.close() # stop generating immediately break response = stream.get_final_message() if steer.interrupt.is_set(): messages.append({"role": "user", "content": "[interrupted by user — awaiting new direction]"}) steer.interrupt.clear() continue # loop back; pick up queued redirect messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content}) if response.stop_reason != "tool_use": break # --- execute tools; honor interrupt between (and inside) calls --- results = [] for tu in (b for b in response.content if b.type == "tool_use"): if steer.interrupt.is_set(): results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": tu.id, "content": "Skipped: run interrupted by user.", "is_error": True}) continue results.append(execute_tool(tu, steer)) # see cancellable bash below messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results}) . The cancellable tool — what to do with a half-finished bash: . import subprocess def execute_tool(tu, steer: Steerable): if tu.name == "bash": proc = subprocess.Popen(tu.input["command"], shell=True, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT, text=True) while proc.poll() is None: if steer.interrupt.is_set(): proc.terminate() # kill the half-finished command return {"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": tu.id, "content": "Command terminated mid-execution by user interrupt.", "is_error": True} # tell the model it did NOT complete time.sleep(0.05) out, _ = proc.communicate() return {"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": tu.id, "content": out} # ... other tools . The key discipline: steering enters the conversation only at loop boundaries, always as appended messages. We never reach in and rewrite the in-flight turn. §5 explains why this is the only clean way, and §6 of the prompt-caching story (Module 10) explains why the cache forces it. 🛠️ Exercise (warm-up): Add the interrupt flag and the queue to Scout. Verify: (a) pressing interrupt mid-bash terminates the subprocess and the model sees an is_error result; (b) a message typed during a tool call shows up as a new user turn at the next boundary, not spliced into the current one. ✅ Self-check: Why feed the model an is_error tool_result on interrupt instead of just dropping the tool call? (Because the message list must reflect reality: every tool_use block needs a matching tool_result, and the model must know the action didn’t complete so it doesn’t assume success on the next turn.) .

199.title: 3. Escalation as a first-class design surface
199.content: The defining question of an autonomous agent is: when does it ASK the human, and when does it just ACT? This is the calibration problem, and it is where most agent products live or die. The clean way to implement “ask” is to make it a tool. Give Scout an ask_human (or request_approval) tool alongside bash and edit. Now asking is a normal action in the agent’s vocabulary — the model decides to call it, the loop blocks for a human answer, and the answer comes back as a tool result. This reframes the human’s role: they move from operator IN the loop (approving every step) to manager ON the exception path (available when the agent decides it needs them). There are two ways to get the calibration wrong, and they fail in opposite directions: . | Asks too much. You’ve quietly rebuilt the human-in-the-loop you were trying to remove. Every action becomes a confirmation prompt; the human becomes a clicking machine; alarm fatigue sets in and they start rubber-stamping without reading — which is worse than no gate, because now the gate gives false assurance. | Asks too little. The agent barrels ahead and commits a costly, possibly irreversible mistake while unattended — a DROP TABLE, an email to the wrong customer, a force-push. The whole point of escalation was to catch exactly this, and it didn’t. | . The calibration axis is the reversibility / blast-radius / confidence triple — and reversibility is the same criterion from Module 11’s gating discussion, reused here as a design knob: . | Signal | Ask | Act | . | Reversibility | Hard/impossible to undo (delete, send, deploy, pay) | Cheaply reversible (read, local edit, scratch file) | . | Blast radius | Affects prod, real users, money, external parties | Affects only the workspace / a sandbox | . | Confidence | Model is uncertain or arguments are ambiguous | Model is confident, action is well-specified | . The escalation tool, with policy baked in: . ASK_HUMAN_TOOL = { "name": "ask_human", "description": ( "Ask the supervising human a question and wait for their answer. " "Call this BEFORE any action that is hard to reverse, affects production " "or real users, or when you are uncertain how to proceed. Do NOT call it " "for reversible, low-blast-radius actions you can confidently take." ), "input_schema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "question": {"type": "string"}, "proposed_action": {"type": "string"}, "reversible": {"type": "boolean", "description": "Whether the proposed action can be cheaply undone."}, }, "required": ["question"], }, } def handle_ask_human(tu, steer: Steerable): q = tu.input["question"] answer = prompt_human(q, proposed=tu.input.get("proposed_action")) # blocks the loop return {"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": tu.id, "content": answer} . Then enforce the policy in the harness too — don’t trust the model to self-gate. Classify each outgoing action by reversibility (the Module 11 classification) and force an approval for the irreversible ones regardless of whether the model asked: . def gate(tu) -> bool: """Return True if this action must be approved by a human before executing.""" if tu.name == "bash": cmd = tu.input["command"] if any(p in cmd for p in ("rm -rf", "git push", "DROP", "curl -X POST", "kubectl delete")): return True # irreversible / high blast radius → always ask if tu.name in ("send_email", "deploy"): return True return False # reversible, low blast radius → act . The art is tuning the ask-rate. Run Scout on a handful of representative tasks, log every ask_human call and every harness-forced gate, and look at the rate. Too high → loosen the descriptions and the gate predicates. Too low and you saw a near-miss → tighten them. This is an eval-able property (Module 08): you can build a small suite of tasks with known “should-ask” / “should-act” labels and measure precision/recall on the escalation decision, exactly like any other classifier. 🛠️ Exercise (escalation): Add ask_human to Scout with the policy above. Run it on three tasks of varying risk. Record the ask-rate. Deliberately mis-tune it once in each direction and feel the failure: an over-asking Scout is exhausting; an under-asking Scout does something you didn’t want. ✅ Self-check: Why enforce reversibility in the harness gate as well as in the tool description? (The description is a soft prompt the model may ignore or miscalibrate; the harness gate is a hard, non-bypassable control. Defense in depth — the same belt-and-suspenders logic as Module 11’s security gating.) .

200.title: 4. Making a long / autonomous run legible
200.content: You let Scout run overnight on a 6-hour task. In the morning, you have a 40,000-line transcript. The question that decides whether this product is usable is: can you understand what it did, and why, in seconds — or do you have to re-read the whole trace? . If the answer is “re-read the trace,” the product is dead on arrival for autonomous use. Nobody audits an overnight run line by line. So you must design legibility in — build a second, human-facing view of the run that is not the raw log. The surfaces that matter: . | A concise progress summary — where the run stands, what’s done, what’s left. | A “what I did and why” decision journal — the key decisions, each with the reasoning, not every tool call. “Chose to skip the staging deploy because the diff was config-only” is a journal entry; ls -la is not. | Surfaced uncertainty — the places the agent was unsure, made an assumption, or guessed. This is gold: it tells the human exactly where to look. | . Why does this matter beyond convenience? Because a human glancing at a well-designed summary and going “wait, that’s not what I meant” is the cheapest drift-detector you have. It catches goal drift (Module 13 — agents wandering off-objective over long unsupervised runs) before any eval can, because the human has the actual intent in their head and the eval only has its proxy. Legibility is not a nicety; it’s an instrument — the human’s eyeball is a sensor, and the summary is what you connect it to. Contrast sharply with the observability traces from Module 09. Those traces are for engineers debugging the agent — spans, token counts, tool latencies, full inputs/outputs. The legibility surface is for the supervising human steering the work — decisions and uncertainty, in their language, at their altitude. Same run, two completely different views, two different audiences. Don’t conflate them; a debugging trace shown as a “summary” is illegible, and a decision journal is useless for debugging a tool-call failure. Implementation: give Scout a tool to write journal entries as it works, and synthesize a summary at the end. The journal entries cost a little context but buy you the entire legibility surface for free. JOURNAL_TOOL = { "name": "log_decision", "description": ( "Record a notable DECISION and the reasoning behind it, or an uncertainty/" "assumption you are making. Use this for choices a supervising human would " "want to review later — not for routine actions." ), "input_schema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "decision": {"type": "string"}, "why": {"type": "string"}, "uncertain": {"type": "boolean"}, }, "required": ["decision", "why"], }, } journal = [] # appended to by handle_log_decision(...) def end_of_run_summary(client, messages, journal): """Synthesize the legibility surface — decisions + uncertainty, not raw logs.""" resp = client.messages.create( model="claude-opus-4-8", max_tokens=1024, messages=messages + [{ "role": "user", "content": ( "Write a concise report for the human who left you running: " "(1) what you did, (2) why — the key decisions, " "(3) what you're UNSURE about or assumed. Decisions, not a log." ), }], ) return {"summary": next(b.text for b in resp.content if b.type == "text"), "decision_journal": journal} . 🛠️ Exercise (legibility): Add log_decision and the end-of-run summary to Scout. Run a multi-step task. Then read only the summary and journal — not the transcript — and ask yourself whether you could catch a goal-drift mistake from them alone. Tune the journal-entry description until the answer is yes. ✅ Self-check: Why is the summary a better drift-detector than an eval? (The human holds the true intent; the eval holds a fixed proxy written in advance. The human catches “that’s not what I meant” — a divergence the eval’s proxy can’t represent because nobody anticipated it.) .

201.title: 5. Inspecting and correcting a live run
201.content: Steering at the boundary (§2) handles redirection. But two harder questions remain, and they’re where the frontier is. INSPECT: can a human see a live run’s state? The honest answer is “not directly.” The agent’s durable state — its message list, scratch files, memory — is optimized for the next model call, not for a human to read. It’s a wall of tool-call JSON and intermediate reasoning. So inspection requires building a second, human-facing projection of that state: the same legibility surface from §4, but rendered live. You don’t show the human the raw state; you show them a view derived from it. This is exactly the read-model / write-model split from CQRS, applied to agents: the write model (durable state) serves the agent; the read model (projection) serves the human. CORRECT: can a human fix a live run’s state mid-flight? This is genuinely hard, and most teams punt on it — for good reasons. Editing a running agent’s state mid-flight is live surgery on a system that has beliefs about itself. If you reach in and change a fact the agent already “knows,” you create an inconsistency between what the agent believes (from earlier in its context) and what is now true. The agent’s later reasoning may still reference the old value; you get incoherence, not correction. Worse, it collides head-on with prompt caching’s append-only / prefix-stable invariant (Module 10). Recall: caching is a prefix match — any byte change anywhere in the cached prefix invalidates everything after it. If you mutate message 5 of a 200-message run, you’ve (a) created the belief inconsistency above and (b) blown away the entire cache from message 5 onward, re-billing the whole tail at full price. The cache is structurally an append-only log; editing the past fights its deepest assumption. So the clean approach is the same one §2 already used, and now you can see why it’s clean: steer by APPENDING an event/message, never by editing past state. Instead of rewriting “source senior candidates” to “source mid-level,” you append: . {"role": "user", "content": "Update: stop sourcing senior candidates. Pivot to mid-level. Ignore the earlier seniority instruction."} . The agent observes this at the next loop boundary, reconciles it against its prior context itself (it’s good at this — that’s what the model is for), and the cached prefix stays byte-stable, so the entire history before the new message is still a cache hit. Append-only steering is correct both as a state-consistency strategy and as a caching strategy. The two constraints point the same direction — which is a strong signal it’s the right design. This append-an-instruction pattern is the same shape platforms standardize: an out-of-band “interrupt” or “user message” event that the orchestrator delivers at a safe boundary, leaving prior history intact. (Some setups even formalize a mid-conversation system message appended to the message list — an operator channel that preserves the cached prefix; see Module 10.) . True live correction — surgically rewriting the agent’s belief mid-turn so it’s instantly consistent and cache-friendly — has no clean general solution. Be honest about this with whoever you’re building for. The pragmatic workaround almost everyone ships: kill the run and restart from a corrected state file. Checkpoint the run (Module 12), let the human edit the checkpoint (which is at rest, so no in-flight inconsistency), and resume from the edited checkpoint. You’re not editing a live agent; you’re editing a paused one and starting fresh. It’s coarse, it’s correct, and it sidesteps both the consistency and the caching problems. ✅ Self-check: Why does appending an instruction preserve the cache while editing message 5 destroys it? (The cache key is the exact byte prefix. Appending leaves the entire prior prefix unchanged → full cache hit on the history. Editing message 5 changes a byte in the prefix → everything from message 5 onward is invalidated and re-billed.) .

202.title: 6. Approval & confirmation UX — deepening the gate

203.title: 7. The audit / review surface — the performance review for your agent
203.content: Everything above is during the run. The audit surface is after: letting a human review what the agent decided and why, retrospectively. Think of it as the performance review for your agent. This ties two earlier modules together into a flywheel: . | It builds on the observability traces (Module 09) — the audit surface is a human-readable rendering of the trace, joined with the decision journal (§4). | It feeds evals (Module 08) — when a human reviews a run and finds a bad decision, that run becomes a new eval case. Human review of production runs is the single richest source of eval data you have. Review → find failure → add eval → fix → review again. The interface closes the loop. | . And underpinning all of it: recoverability is part of the interface. The audit surface is only valuable if, having found a mistake, the human can undo it. So recoverability is a design requirement, not an afterthought: . | Git for everything the agent touches — every edit is a commit, so every edit is one git revert away. | Dry-runs and previews (§6) — catch the mistake before it commits. | Confirmations on irreversible actions (§3) — the things git can’t undo (sent email, deployed code, charged card) get the hard gate. | . The throughline of the whole module lands here: making mistakes survivable is what lets users grant autonomy. A user who knows any bad action is one revert away will let the agent run on far more, because their downside is bounded. Recoverability doesn’t reduce the rate of mistakes — that’s the reliability problem — it reduces their cost, which is the trust problem. Two sides of the same coin, again.

204.title: 8. Adoption & trust dynamics in regulated / outward-facing domains
204.content: Sharpen the stakes. For an internal coding agent, a mistake costs some rework. For an outward-facing or regulated agent — recruiting, customer support, finance, healthcare — a wrong autonomous action is expensive and accountable: a discriminatory candidate rejection, a wrong financial figure quoted to a customer, a HIPAA-relevant disclosure. Here the model’s reliability is not the safety story, because you can never get it to zero and the cost of the residual is too high to eat. The interface and recoverability are the safety mechanism. In these domains: . | The escalation surface (§3) is where regulatory and policy judgment enters — anything with legal or financial consequence routes to a human by design, not by the model’s discretion. | The audit surface (§7) is the accountability record — who decided what, when, why, and who approved it. In a regulated domain this isn’t a nicety; it’s a compliance requirement. | Recoverability bounds the blast radius of the residual errors you can’t eliminate. | . The autonomy a user (or an institution) grants is exactly the function we opened with: a function of how cheap inspection is and how survivable mistakes are. In a regulated domain both terms are scrutinized hard — inspection has to satisfy an auditor, and “survivable” has to satisfy a regulator. Which is precisely why, for these agents, the human-interface layer is the product, and the model is the commodity underneath it.

205.title: 🛠️ Exercise: a human-interface layer for Scout
205.content: Build all of the following onto Scout’s loop (Module 03) and its permission gate (Modules 03/11). Keep Scout framework-free. After each part, write in notes.md how that surface changed your willingness to let Scout run unattended — that subjective shift is the actual deliverable. (a) Plan mode (dry-run). Before executing a task, Scout first proposes a step-by-step plan and waits for approval. Only on approval does it run the loop. Implement the propose → approve → execute gate. (b) Interruptible execution. Let the user interrupt mid-run (Ctrl-C or a typed message) and inject a redirect that Scout picks up at the next loop boundary, without killing the run. Implement the queue + interrupt flag from §2, including the cancellable bash. (c) Legibility surface. After a run, Scout emits a concise “what I did / why / what I’m unsure about” summary plus a decision journal — not the raw transcript. Use log_decision + end_of_run_summary from §4. (d) Calibrated escalation. Add ask_human with a policy: ask on irreversible / ambiguous / low-confidence actions, act on reversible ones (reuse the Module 11 reversibility classification). Run Scout on a few tasks, measure the ask-rate, and tune it. (e) Approval UX. When Scout proposes a write/bash action, render the action + a preview/diff + blast radius, and remember “always allow X for this session.” Deepen the Module 03 gate per §6. (f) Stretch — autonomy dial. Add a read-only / auto-edit / full-auto dial the user sets per run that changes which actions are auto-allowed vs. gated. Confirm the irreversible class is gated at every level. Reflect in notes.md: which single surface most increased your willingness to walk away while Scout worked? For most people it’s plan mode or one-keystroke interrupt — notice why.

206.title: Real production issues
206.content: . | The demo-to-trust gap. The agent demos beautifully and then stalls the moment a human has to oversee it for real. The fix was never a better model — it’s steering, approval previews, legibility, and undo. Teams that treat UX as “later” ship demos, not products. | Ask-rate miscalibration → alarm fatigue. Too many confirmations and the human rubber-stamps blindly, which is worse than no gate because it manufactures false confidence. Too few and the agent commits an unattended irreversible mistake. Calibrate by reversibility/blast-radius; make the gate an eval-able classifier (§3). | Illegible long runs. You can’t tell what an overnight run did, so you can’t catch drift, so you can’t trust it overnight — a vicious circle. The decision journal + summary (§4) is the way out; the raw trace is not. | Can’t inspect or correct a live run. Durable state is built for the agent, not the human, and true mid-run correction has no clean solution. Ship the read-model projection for inspection and the kill-and-restart-from-checkpoint workaround for correction; don’t promise live surgery you can’t deliver. | Over-automation. Removing the human before the agent has earned the trust — defaulting to full-auto out of the gate. Earn autonomy with the dial; start gated, loosen as the human watches it succeed. | Steering that fights the cache. Implementing “correction” by editing past messages blows the prompt cache (Module 10) and creates belief inconsistency. Append events at boundaries; never rewrite history. | Regulated/outward-facing reality. For these agents the interface + recoverability are the safety mechanism, not model reliability — and the audit surface is a compliance artifact, not a convenience. | . The thread that ties every one of these back to the thesis: each is a place where insufficient reliability had to be covered by interaction design, and the failure is what happens when the interface wasn’t there to catch it. The reliability problem and the UX problem are the same problem. You manage what you couldn’t make perfect by building the boundary where the human and the agent meet. In Module 12 these surfaces stop being toy loop-hooks and become real infrastructure: streaming over SSE to a UI, durable suspend/resume that makes pause-for-approval natural (a run can wait days for a human and resume exactly where it left off), and checkpoints that make kill-and-restart-from-corrected-state a first-class operation rather than a hack.

207.title: Check yourself
207.content: . | State the module’s thesis in one sentence, and explain why “the reliability problem and the UX problem are two sides of the same coin.” | Why is instant, safe interruption disproportionately important for how much autonomy a user will grant? | Give the two failure directions of escalation miscalibration and the signal you calibrate on to avoid both. | Why is a human glancing at a run summary a cheaper drift-detector than an eval — and what can it catch that the eval can’t? | Why does correcting a live run by appending a message preserve the prompt cache while editing a past message destroys it? Connect this to Module 10’s prefix invariant. | Explain why plan mode is described as “the single highest-trust pattern.” | Why does the irreversible-action class stay gated even at the full-auto autonomy level? | For a regulated, outward-facing agent, why are the interface and recoverability — not model reliability — the actual safety mechanism? | .

208.title: Further reading
208.content: . | Module 03 — the agent loop and the permission gate (the foundation everything here hooks into). | Module 10 — prompt caching’s append-only / prefix-stable invariant (why steering must append, never edit). | Module 09 — observability traces (the engineer-facing view; contrast with the human-facing legibility surface here). | Module 08 — evals (human review of runs feeds new eval cases — the flywheel of §7). | Module 11 — security, HITL, and the reversibility criterion (reused here as the escalation calibration axis). | Module 13 — long-running agents and goal drift (what the legibility surface is built to catch early). | Agent platforms as evidence the primitives are standard: Anthropic’s Managed Agents expose interrupt events, tool-confirmation round-trips, and SSE event streams; Claude Code and Cursor expose plan mode, auto-accept/autonomy levels, and one-keystroke interrupt. The patterns in this module are conceptual reimplementations of surfaces these products ship. | . → Next: Module 12 — Deployment & Durable Execution .

210.title: Module 12 — Deployment & Durable Execution
210.content: Everything so far has assumed Scout runs in a terminal. You type a task, the loop spins, you read the answer, the process exits. That’s a fine place to learn an agent, and a terrible place to operate one. The moment an agent has to serve more than one caller, survive longer than a request timeout, or pick up tomorrow where it left off today, you’re no longer writing an agent — you’re writing a distributed system whose request handler happens to be stochastic and slow. You already know how to operate distributed systems. The new material here is small but it’s exactly the part your intuition will misfile. An agent’s “handler” runs for minutes to hours, not milliseconds. Its “request” is a growing transcript that is the application state. Its side effects are real (it sends emails, opens PRs, deletes files), it’s non-deterministic, and any individual step can fail transiently — model rate limits, a sandbox eviction, a deploy that rolls your process. The good news: the patterns that make this tractable are ones you already trust. Statelessness. Event sourcing. Idempotency. Sagas. Replay. This module is about mapping those onto agents and then reaching for the production answer — durable execution — when run duration outgrows a single process.

211.title: Learning objectives
211.content: By the end of this module you should be able to: . | Place a given agent workload on the script → sync API → async job → persistent agent spectrum, and pick the deployment shape its run duration demands. | Explain why the harness, not the model, owns all state — and externalize that state durably as an append-only event log (event sourcing applied to a stochastic handler). | Reason about the brain / hands / session split and why the session (the log) is the source of truth, not the process memory. | Survive the “discrete sessions with amnesia” problem with the initializer / worker pattern: continuity lives in files, not context. | Describe what a durable execution engine (Temporal; LangGraph checkpointing) buys you — journal-and-replay resumption — and the one footgun it forces you to confront (non-idempotent side effects on replay). | Choose between hosted (Anthropic Managed Agents) and self-hosted (your loop + Temporal/LangGraph + a sandbox vendor), and name the tradeoffs. | Implement checkpoint + resume for Scout, and a FastAPI service that streams its events. | . 📖 This module is the infrastructure. Module 13 is the persistent-agent concept — what an agent that runs for days against an ongoing goal can become. Here we build the floor it stands on.

212.title: 1. From script to service: the spectrum
212.content: There is no single “deploy an agent” answer because there is no single agent. The deployment shape is dictated almost entirely by one variable: how long does a run take? That number decides whether the run can live inside an HTTP request, must move to a background worker, or must outlive the process entirely. | Shape | Run duration | Where it lives | State concern | . | (a) CLI / script | seconds–minutes | one process, foreground | in-memory; dies with the process | . | (b) Sync request/response API | seconds–~minute | inside an HTTP request | in-memory per request; must stream | . | (c) Async background job | minutes–hours | queue + worker pool | externalized; survives the request | . | (d) Long-running / persistent agent | hours–days | a durable workflow | append-only log is the source of truth | . Scout today is (a). Most of this module is about earning your way down the table. The jump from (a) to (b) is mechanical: wrap the loop in a handler. The jump from (b) to (c) is the one that breaks naive designs — a 40-minute agent run cannot block an HTTP connection (load balancers, proxies, and clients all give up around 30–120s), so the run must detach from the request and report progress out-of-band. The jump from (c) to (d) is the one this module spends the most time on, because “the process might die in the middle and that has to be fine” is a property you have to design for, not bolt on. A deployment shape: FastAPI wrapping Scout with streaming . Here is shape (b)/(c) for Scout: a service that accepts a task, runs the loop in the background, and streams events (via Server-Sent Events) to the client as they happen, keyed by a session_id, with an endpoint to interrupt a run mid-flight. Streaming isn’t a nicety here — a multi-minute run with no output looks identical to a hung server, and (callback to Module 1) the Anthropic API itself wants streaming for any long call so you don’t hit request timeouts. # service.py — FastAPI front end for Scout import asyncio, json, uuid from fastapi import FastAPI from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse from pydantic import BaseModel app = FastAPI() # session_id -> live run handle. In-memory here for clarity; in production this # is Redis or a DB so multiple service replicas can find a run (see §2). RUNS: dict[str, "Run"] = {} class Run: def __init__(self, session_id: str, task: str): self.session_id = session_id self.task = task self.queue: asyncio.Queue = asyncio.Queue() # events out to the client self.interrupt = asyncio.Event() # steering: stop signal in class StartReq(BaseModel): task: str @app.post("/runs") async def start_run(req: StartReq): session_id = str(uuid.uuid4()) run = Run(session_id, req.task) RUNS[session_id] = run asyncio.create_task(_drive(run)) # detach from the request return {"session_id": session_id} @app.get("/runs/{session_id}/events") async def stream_events(session_id: str): run = RUNS[session_id] async def sse(): while True: event = await run.queue.get() yield f"data: {json.dumps(event)}\n\n" if event["type"] in ("done", "error", "interrupted"): break return StreamingResponse(sse(), media_type="text/event-stream") @app.post("/runs/{session_id}/interrupt") async def interrupt_run(session_id: str): RUNS[session_id].interrupt.set() # the loop checks this each iteration return {"ok": True} async def _drive(run: Run): try: # scout_loop is an async generator that yields events and checks # run.interrupt at the top of each iteration (see below). async for event in scout_loop(run.task, interrupt=run.interrupt): await run.queue.put(event) await run.queue.put({"type": "done"}) except asyncio.CancelledError: await run.queue.put({"type": "interrupted"}) except Exception as e: await run.queue.put({"type": "error", "message": str(e)}) . The Module 3 loop becomes an async generator that emits an event per meaningful step and honors the interrupt flag: . # scout_async.py — the loop, instrumented to stream and to be steerable import anthropic async_client = anthropic.AsyncAnthropic() async def scout_loop(task: str, interrupt): messages = [{"role": "user", "content": task}] system = build_system_prompt() for step in range(MAX_ITERS): if interrupt.is_set(): return # steering: bail cleanly async with async_client.messages.stream( model="claude-opus-4-8", max_tokens=4096, system=system, tools=[t.to_schema() for t in TOOLS], messages=messages, ) as stream: async for text in stream.text_stream: yield {"type": "token", "text": text} # live tokens to the UI resp = await stream.get_final_message() messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content}) if resp.stop_reason != "tool_use": yield {"type": "final", "text": "".join(b.text for b in resp.content if b.type == "text")} return results = [dispatch(b) for b in resp.content if b.type == "tool_use"] for b in resp.content: if b.type == "tool_use": yield {"type": "tool_use", "name": b.name, "input": b.input} messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results}) . This service is real, and for short interactive runs it’s enough. But notice what’s load-bearing and fragile: messages lives in process memory. If this worker is OOM-killed at step 30 of a 50-step task, the run is gone. There is no resume. That single fact is what the rest of the module is about. ✅ Checkpoint: You can run Scout behind an HTTP API that streams tokens and tool-use events to a client, with a session id and an interrupt endpoint. You have not yet made a run survive the process dying.

213.title: 2. State is the central problem
213.content: Lean on your intuition here, because it’s exactly right: the model is a stateless function. Every messages.create call is pure — same inputs, (roughly) same output distribution; the API server remembers nothing about your previous call (Module 1). All the state that makes an agent an agent — the transcript, the working directory, scratch memory, open tool sessions — lives in the harness, the code you wrote around the model. That has a sharp consequence. For a single request, in-memory state is fine; the request and the state are born and die together. For anything that must outlive a single request — a job that runs across a deploy, an agent that resumes tomorrow — you must externalize the state durably. This is not an agent-specific insight. It’s the same move that took web tiers from sticky-session stateful boxes to stateless app servers backed by a database. The app server can die and be replaced; the session lives in Postgres. We are going to do exactly that to Scout: make the worker disposable and move the run into durable storage. The brain / hands / session split . The convergent architecture for serious long-running agents (Anthropic’s framing, and most practitioners’) decomposes the harness into three parts with very different durability requirements: . ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ BRAIN — model + loop (stateless, restartable) │ │ decides the next action from the current log │ └───────────────┬──────────────────────────┬──────────────┘ │ tool calls │ append events ▼ ▼ ┌──────────────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────────────┐ │ HANDS — ephemeral │ │ SESSION — append-only │ │ sandboxed execution │ │ EVENT LOG │ │ (Module 11): bash, files │ │ the durable source │ │ disposable, rebuildable │ │ of truth │ └──────────────────────────┘ └──────────────────────────┘ . | Brain — the model plus your loop. Stateless and restartable. Given the current log, it produces the next action. If the process dies, you spin up a new brain and hand it the same log. | Hands — the ephemeral, sandboxed place where tool calls actually run (Module 11’s territory: a container, a microVM). Disposable by design. Its contents are derived state — anything important the hands produce gets recorded in the session. | Session — an append-only event log that is the single durable source of truth. Every user message, model response, tool call, and tool result is an immutable entry. Recovery means: rebuild a brain, replay/reload the log, continue. | . If “append-only log that is the source of truth, from which you reconstruct current state” sounds familiar, it should: this is event sourcing, applied to a handler that happens to be a language model. Name the analogy and the rest follows. The transcript isn’t a convenience buffer you keep around for the model’s benefit — it’s the event store. Current state (the messages array, the cursor into the task) is a projection you fold from the log. And the log gives you the two things event sourcing always gives you: recovery (replay to reconstruct) and audit (a complete, immutable record of exactly what the agent did and why — which, for an autonomous system taking real actions, you will be very glad to have). 📖 The bridge from Module 4: there we treated files as memory to fit a task into a finite context window. Here the same idea does double duty — files and the event log are how state survives a process boundary, not just a context boundary. Files-as-memory is the thing that makes durability possible. Hold that thought; §3 leans on it hard.

214.title: 3. Discrete sessions with amnesia
214.content: Here is the reality that trips up everyone coming from request/response systems. A long-running agent does not run in one continuous, ever-growing context. It runs as a sequence of discrete sessions, each bounded by a context window and, often, a process lifetime. A multi-day task is not one 9,000,000-token conversation. It’s hundreds of sessions, each of which starts with no memory of the last. The agent has amnesia at every session boundary. (Module 13 will treat this as a feature to design around; here it’s the constraint that forces our hand.) . So where does continuity live? Not in context — context is reset every session. It has to live in files and durable state the next session can read. This is the §2 bridge made concrete: the stateless-web-tier-plus-database pattern, one layer down. Each session is a stateless worker; the filesystem and event log are the database; a fresh session rehydrates from disk and carries on. Anthropic’s pattern for this is a clean two-role split: . | The initializer agent runs once, on first start. It sets up the environment and writes the durable artifacts the workers will depend on: a PLAN.md (the goal, broken into steps), an empty progress.log, any scaffolding (a repo cloned, a venv built, fixtures fetched). It is the constructor. | The worker agent runs every subsequent session. It does the same four things every time: (1) read PLAN.md and progress.log to figure out where things stand, (2) do the next increment of work, (3) record what it did and learned by appending to progress.log and updating state files, (4) leave clear artifacts so its successor — which shares none of its context — can pick up cleanly. It is the request handler, and it’s stateless. | . session 1 (initializer): write PLAN.md, init progress.log, scaffold env session 2 (worker): read PLAN+progress → do step 1 → append progress, commit session 3 (worker): read PLAN+progress → do step 2 → append progress, commit … (each session amnesiac; continuity is on disk) session N (worker): read PLAN+progress → all steps done → write RESULT.md . The discipline this imposes on prompts and tools is the real work. The worker’s system prompt must insist on the read-first / record-last ritual, because a worker that forgets to write its progress has, from its successor’s point of view, done nothing — the next session will redo it. The artifacts must be written for a reader with no shared context: “fixed the bug” is useless; “step 3 (parser): fixed off-by-one in tokenize(), line 88; tests green; next: step 4, wire up the CLI flag” is a handoff. You are, in effect, writing the agent’s commit messages for it to read. 📖 This is the conceptual core that Module 13 builds the persistent-agent vision on top of. The infrastructure point for this module: continuity is a file/state design problem, not a context-window problem. No bigger context window makes the amnesia go away — only durable artifacts do.

215.title: 4. Durable execution: the production answer to long-running reliability
215.content: Now the hard part. You have a 3-hour agentic run. It fails at step 47 of 60 — a rate-limit storm, a transient sandbox eviction, a deploy that rolled the worker out from under it. It must not restart from step 1. Re-running 46 expensive, slow, side-effecting steps to get back to where you were is unacceptable on cost, on latency, and (if those steps had side effects) on correctness. Crash recovery for a multi-hour stochastic process is the problem durable execution exists to solve. The mechanism will be deeply familiar, because it’s a write-ahead log plus replay — the same primitive under every database’s crash recovery. A durable execution engine journals every step as an immutable event to durable storage as it happens. On failure, it doesn’t restart your workflow; it replays the event history, feeding each already-completed step its recorded result instead of re-executing it, until it reaches the step that hadn’t finished — and resumes there. The 46 completed steps are not re-run; their results are replayed from the journal in milliseconds. This is your saga / workflow-engine intuition, applied to an agent loop. Temporal — the canonical engine . Temporal is the engine most serious long-running agents use; OpenAI runs it for Codex, and Replit, Lovable, and others build on it. (It raised $300M at a $5B valuation in early 2026, which tells you how central durable execution has become to this space.) The OpenAI Agents SDK ships a GA Temporal integration. Temporal’s model is “workflow as code.” You write your orchestration as ordinary code; Temporal makes it durable by recording every step’s result to an event history and replaying that history to reconstruct state after any failure. Two concepts: . | Workflow — your orchestration logic. It must be deterministic, because Temporal re-executes it during replay and the re-execution must follow the exact same path. So a workflow may not do I/O, call time.now(), or hit the network directly. (Sound restrictive? It’s the same constraint as a pure reducer folding an event log — and for the same reason.) | Activity — a unit of non-deterministic, side-effecting work: a model call, a tool call, anything that touches the outside world. Temporal records each activity’s result in the history. On replay, completed activities are not re-run — their recorded result is handed back. | . The mapping onto an agent is direct: the model call is an activity; each tool call is an activity; the loop that strings them together is the workflow. A tiny conceptual sketch (Temporal Python, illustrative): . from temporalio import workflow, activity @activity.defn async def model_step(messages: list) -> dict: # The one non-deterministic thing in the loop. Its result is journaled. resp = await async_client.messages.create( model="claude-opus-4-8", max_tokens=4096, system=SYSTEM, tools=TOOL_SCHEMAS, messages=messages) return resp.model_dump() @activity.defn async def run_tool(name: str, args: dict) -> str: return dispatch_tool(name, args) # side effects happen HERE, journaled @workflow.defn class ScoutWorkflow: @workflow.run async def run(self, task: str) -> str: messages = [{"role": "user", "content": task}] for _ in range(MAX_ITERS): resp = await workflow.execute_activity( model_step, messages, start_to_close_timeout=TIMEOUT) messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp["content"]}) tool_uses = [b for b in resp["content"] if b["type"] == "tool_use"] if not tool_uses: return final_text(resp) results = [] for tu in tool_uses: out = await workflow.execute_activity( run_tool, tu["name"], tu["input"], start_to_close_timeout=TIMEOUT) results.append(tool_result(tu["id"], out)) messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results}) . Crash at iteration 47? Temporal spins up a fresh worker, replays the history (46 model_step and their run_tool results come back instantly from the journal, no API calls, no re-execution), and the loop continues at iteration 47 as if nothing happened. You wrote a for loop; you got crash-proof resumption. That is the whole pitch. LangGraph checkpointing — the lighter-weight, in-framework alternative . If you’re already in LangGraph (Module 7), you don’t need a separate engine for a large class of cases. LangGraph models the agent as a state graph and offers a checkpointer that persists the graph’s state after every node transition to a backing store (in-memory, SQLite, Postgres). Attach one and you get: . | Resume — pass the same thread_id and the graph rehydrates from its last checkpoint and continues from the node it stopped at. | Time-travel — load any prior checkpoint and branch a new run from it. Invaluable for debugging a long agent (“re-run from the state right before it deleted the file”) and for human steering. | . from langgraph.checkpoint.sqlite import SqliteSaver graph = build_scout_graph().compile(checkpointer=SqliteSaver.from_conn_string("scout.db")) cfg = {"configurable": {"thread_id": session_id}} graph.invoke({"task": task}, cfg) # crash, then re-invoke with the same thread_id → resumes . LangGraph Platform packages this for deployment (managed runs, persistence, a streaming API). The tradeoff vs Temporal: LangGraph’s checkpointing is lighter to adopt and tightly integrated with the graph model, but it’s checkpoint-of-state, not journal-and-replay of every step; for very long, very high-stakes orchestration with complex retry/timeout/compensation needs, Temporal’s model is more battle-tested. Inngest and Restate occupy similar ground — durable functions/workflows with journaling — and are worth a look if you want durable execution without adopting the full Temporal operational footprint. ✅ The shape to remember: journal every step → on failure, replay the journal to skip completed work → resume at the failure. It’s a saga with a write-ahead log. Whatever engine you pick, that’s what you’re buying.

216.title: 5. Human-in-the-loop, at the infrastructure level
216.content: Module 11 made the case for human approval on dangerous actions. Durable execution makes implementing it natural, because pausing-and-waiting is just another kind of “this step isn’t done yet.” An agent that needs an approval can suspend, persist its entire state, and resume when a human responds — and crucially, it can wait for hours or days without holding a process, a thread, or a connection open. The waiting state lives in the journal, not in memory. In Temporal this is a workflow that blocks on a signal: the workflow reaches an approval step, parks (durably — you could deploy through the wait and it survives), and resumes the instant a POST /approve delivers the signal. In LangGraph it’s an interrupt before a node: the graph checkpoints, returns control, and resumes on the next invoke with the human’s decision. Either way, escalation/approval becomes a first-class durable step, not a hack with a polling loop and a sleep. The agent that asks “may I delete this production table?” and waits a day for a human to say yes — without burning a single token or process while it waits — is a direct payoff of durable execution.

217.title: 6. Hosted vs self-hosted
217.content: You now have two ways to run a durable, long-lived agent in production. Self-host the whole thing. Your loop, your durable execution engine (Temporal / LangGraph / Inngest / Restate), and a sandbox vendor for the hands — E2B, Modal, Daytona, or raw Firecracker microVMs (Module 11). Maximum control, maximum ops burden: you operate the workflow engine, the worker pool, the sandbox fleet, the autoscaling, the upgrades. This is the right call when you need deep control over the loop, custom tools, specific compliance/residency, or you’re running at a scale where margins matter. Use Anthropic Managed Agents. Anthropic runs the loop and hosts a per-session sandbox container for you. The flow (verified, from Module-1’s API surface) is: create an Agent once (model, system prompt, tools — a persisted, versioned config) → create a Session per run → stream events back over SSE while you send messages and tool results in. Anthropic runs the brain loop and provisions the hands (the per-session container) on its infrastructure. It supports scheduled deployments (run an agent on a cron cadence — the platform’s answer to “run this every night”), and self-hosted sandboxes are an option if you want the loop hosted but the hands on your own infra. You own state in the sense that matters — the API is stateless and the session log is yours — but you don’t run the orchestration. The tradeoff is the usual hosted-vs-self-hosted axis, sharpened by how new and fast-moving this layer is: . |   | Self-hosted (loop + Temporal/LangGraph + sandbox vendor) | Hosted (Managed Agents) | . | Control over loop/tools | total | bounded by the platform | . | Ops burden | you run engine + sandbox fleet | Anthropic runs it | . | Lock-in | low (portable workflow code) | higher (platform-shaped) | . | Time to production | slower | fast (create agent → session) | . | Best when | deep control, scale, custom infra | speed, less ops, standard shapes | . Neither is “correct.” A team shipping a standard coding-assistant flow should probably start hosted and not build a Temporal cluster. A team whose agent is the product, running at scale with bespoke tools, will likely self-host. Most importantly: the concepts — brain/hands/session, the event log, journal-and-replay, idempotent side effects — are identical across both. Pick the operations model; the engineering doesn’t change.

218.title: 7. Operational concerns
218.content: Durability fixes “the process died.” It surfaces a set of problems that didn’t exist when runs were ephemeral. Idempotency of side effects across replays — the one that bites everyone. This is the single most important paragraph in the module. Replay re-drives your workflow code, and replaying a step that already ran must not run its side effect again. If run_tool("send_email", …) succeeded and was journaled, but a crash happened before the workflow recorded the next step, recovery will pass back the recorded result — good. But if you wrote a side effect in the deterministic workflow body instead of inside an activity, replay will execute it again — and your customer gets the email twice. The rule: all side effects go inside journaled activities (or are otherwise made idempotent), never in the replayed workflow body. And belt-and-suspenders: make the effect itself idempotent with a key, so even a duplicated delivery is a no-op. A non-idempotent side effect re-firing on replay is the canonical durable-execution footgun (more in §Real production issues). Observability of long runs (Module 9). A multi-hour run that you can’t see inside of is a multi-hour outage waiting to happen. The event log is your friend here — it’s already a structured, append-only trace. Emit spans per step, surface per-run cost and progress, and make “where is run X right now and what has it done” a one-query answer. Cost over long runs (Module 10). An agent with no budget and no timeout is a way to spend money in your sleep. Every long-running agent needs a hard token budget and a wall-clock timeout, enforced by the harness — a runaway or looping agent burning tokens unattended at 3 a.m. is a real and expensive failure mode. Cap iterations, cap dollars, cap time. Versioning while runs are in flight. You deploy a new system prompt. Runs started yesterday are mid-flight on the old prompt, their journals full of the old behavior. Changing the prompt under a replaying workflow can break determinism outright. Durable engines have explicit answers (Temporal’s workflow versioning / patching; pinning a run to an agent version, exactly as Managed Agents does). The point: an in-flight run is bound to the agent version it started under. Plan for old runs draining on old configs. Graceful shutdown and resume across deploys. Because state is in the journal, a deploy is no longer a catastrophe — drain workers, let the engine reschedule in-flight runs onto fresh workers, resume from the journal. This is the payoff for all the discipline above: deploys, scale-downs, and spot-instance evictions stop being incidents and become routine. That’s the whole reason you externalized the state.

219.title: 🛠️ Exercise: Deploy & durabilize Scout
219.content: Goal: an agent that survives a crash and resumes. You’ll wrap Scout in a service, give it a durable event log keyed by session, prove resumption by killing the process mid-run, implement the initializer/worker pattern, and make one tool side effect idempotent. (a) Wrap Scout in a streaming FastAPI service . Stand up the service from §1: POST /runs starts a run (detached from the request) and returns a session_id; GET /runs/{session_id}/events streams events as SSE; POST /runs/{session_id}/interrupt sets the steering flag the loop checks each iteration. Convert Scout’s loop to the async generator shown in §1 so it yields token / tool_use / final events. Test: start a run in one terminal, curl -N the events endpoint in another, and confirm you see tokens and tool-use events stream in, and that hitting interrupt stops the run cleanly. (b) Make Scout’s state durable: checkpoint + resume . This is the heart of the exercise. Give Scout an append-only event log on disk, keyed by session_id, written after each step, so a restarted process can reload it and continue. # checkpoint.py — the session log is the source of truth (event sourcing) import json, os def log_path(session_id): return f"sessions/{session_id}.jsonl" def append_event(session_id, event: dict): os.makedirs("sessions", exist_ok=True) with open(log_path(session_id), "a") as f: f.write(json.dumps(event) + "\n") f.flush(); os.fsync(f.fileno()) # durable before we proceed def load_messages(session_id) -> list: """Fold the event log back into a messages array (a projection).""" if not os.path.exists(log_path(session_id)): return [] messages = [] for line in open(log_path(session_id)): ev = json.loads(line) if ev["type"] == "user": messages.append({"role": "user", "content": ev["content"]}) elif ev["type"] == "assistant": messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": ev["content"]}) elif ev["type"] == "tool_results": messages.append({"role": "user", "content": ev["content"]}) return messages . Now make Scout’s loop resumable: on start, load_messages(session_id); if it’s empty, this is a fresh run, so append the user task; otherwise it’s a resume, so continue from the rebuilt messages. After every model response and every batch of tool results, append_event before doing anything else. The invariant: the on-disk log always reflects completed steps, so a reload never loses or duplicates a step. def run_resumable(session_id: str, task: str | None): messages = load_messages(session_id) if not messages: # fresh run append_event(session_id, {"type": "user", "content": task}) messages = load_messages(session_id) while len(messages) < MAX_ITERS * 2: resp = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=4096, system=build_system_prompt(), tools=TOOL_SCHEMAS, messages=messages) append_event(session_id, {"type": "assistant", "content": serialize(resp.content)}) messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content}) if resp.stop_reason != "tool_use": return final_text(resp) results = [dispatch(b) for b in resp.content if b.type == "tool_use"] append_event(session_id, {"type": "tool_results", "content": results}) messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results}) . Test the resume — this is the point of the whole module. Start a multi-step task (the “fix the bug in buggy.py” task from Module 3 works; pad it so it takes several steps). Kill the process with Ctrl-C (or kill -9) partway through. Then re-run with the same session_id and no task. Scout should reload the log, skip the work it already did, and finish from where it stopped. Verify by diffing the event logs of an uninterrupted run and a killed-and-resumed run: same final state, no duplicated steps. (c) Implement the initializer / worker pattern . Split a longer task across multiple “sessions.” Write an initializer that runs once and produces PLAN.md (the task as an ordered checklist) and an empty progress.log. Write a worker session whose system prompt requires it to: read PLAN.md + progress.log, do exactly one unchecked step, append a clear handoff line to progress.log, and stop. Run the worker repeatedly (each invocation a fresh process — the amnesia is real) until PLAN.md is fully checked off. The deliverable: a task completed across N amnesiac sessions where the only thing carried between them is on disk. (d) Make one tool side effect idempotent . Pick a side-effecting tool (write_file is fine; a mock send_notification is better because the double-fire is visible). Give the operation an idempotency key — for write_file, the target path + a content hash; for send_notification, a caller-supplied idempotency_key. Keep a small on-disk set of keys already executed. On invocation, if the key is present, return the recorded result without re-executing. Then simulate a replay: feed the same tool call twice and prove the effect happens once. This is the §7 footgun, defused. (e) Stretch: sketch it as a durable workflow . Take your resumable loop from (b) and rewrite it as either a Temporal workflow (model call and each tool call as activities, per §4) or a LangGraph graph with a checkpointer. You don’t need to run a Temporal cluster — a faithful sketch is enough. Then write one paragraph answering: what did the durable execution engine give me for free that I hand-rolled in (b)? (Answers should include: journaling and replay you didn’t write, retry/timeout/backoff per activity, the suspend-for-human-approval primitive from §5, versioning of in-flight runs, and graceful resume across deploys.) .

220.title: Real production issues
220.content: . | Runs lost to crashes, rate-limit storms, and deploys — for want of durability. The default failure mode of the §1 service: a worker dies at step 30 and the run is simply gone, with no resume. A deploy mid-run, a 529 storm, a spot eviction — all total losses. Durability (§2–4) is the fix, and the reason it’s not optional at scale. | Non-idempotent side effects double-firing on replay — the #1 durable-execution footgun. A step sends an email, the workflow crashes before recording it, replay sends the email again. Or a side effect written in the replayed workflow body instead of a journaled activity fires on every replay. This is the bug that turns “durable execution saved us” into “durable execution emailed every customer three times.” Side effects go in activities; effects get idempotency keys (Exercise (d)). | State drift across sessions: the successor misreads stale artifacts. A worker writes an ambiguous or out-of-date progress.log line; the next amnesiac session reads it, misjudges where things stand, and redoes or skips work. The fix is discipline in how artifacts are written (write for a reader with zero shared context) plus treating the log as append-only truth, not a mutable scratchpad. | Hung / runaway background agents burning tokens unattended. An agent with no timeout and no budget loops at 3 a.m. and bills you for it (Module 10). Every background run needs a hard token budget, a wall-clock cap, and an iteration cap, enforced by the harness — and an alert when it trips them. | Versioning an agent mid-flight: in-flight runs on old prompts. You ship a new system prompt; runs started before the deploy are mid-journal on the old behavior, and replaying them under the new prompt breaks determinism or changes the agent’s mind mid-task. Pin runs to the agent version they began on; let old runs drain. | The hosted-vs-self-hosted lock-in / control tradeoff. Hosted (Managed Agents) gets you to production fast and off the ops treadmill, at the cost of control and some platform lock-in. Self-hosting (Temporal/LangGraph + a sandbox vendor) gives you total control and portability, at the cost of running the whole stack. The concepts port across both — choose on operations, not architecture. | Sandbox provisioning cost and latency at scale (the hands layer). A per-session container that takes seconds to provision and costs money to keep warm is fine for one agent and a real bill for ten thousand. The hands layer (E2B/Modal/Daytona/Firecracker) is where long-running-agent infra cost and cold-start latency actually live — pool, pre-warm, and cap aggressively. | Observability of multi-hour runs. You cannot debug what you cannot see. Lean on the event log as a native trace, emit per-step spans and per-run cost/progress (Module 9), and make “where is this run and what has it done” answerable without grepping logs. | “Discrete sessions with amnesia” means continuity is a file/state design problem. The deepest one. No context window is big enough to make a multi-day agent into one conversation; continuity must live in durable artifacts that an amnesiac successor can read. If you design the agent assuming a continuous memory it doesn’t have, it will silently forget across every session boundary. | .

221.title: Check yourself
221.content: . | Scout’s run dies at step 30 of 50 and resumes from step 1. Which architectural property is missing, and what’s the minimal change (from §2) that fixes it? | Explain the brain/hands/session split. Which of the three is the durable source of truth, and which two are disposable — and why is that exactly the event-sourcing pattern? | Why must a Temporal workflow be deterministic while activities may not be? Map that distinction onto Scout’s model call and tool calls. | A durable run replays after a crash and your customer receives the same email twice. Name the two distinct mistakes that could cause this, and the fix for each. | A long agent has amnesia at every session boundary. Where does continuity live, and why won’t a bigger context window solve it? Describe the initializer/worker handoff. | You deploy a new system prompt while a 2-hour run is in flight on the old one. What can break, and what’s the standard mitigation? | For a 30-second interactive coding turn vs an overnight multi-step refactor, how does the right deployment shape (§1) differ, and why? | What does a durable execution engine give you “for free” that you’d otherwise hand-roll? List four things. | .

222.content: . | Module 3 — the loop you’re now wrapping, streaming, and making resumable. | Module 4 — files-as-memory: the bridge from context management to durability. | Module 9 — observability: the event log doubles as your trace for long runs. | Module 10 — reliability, cost, and budgets/timeouts for unattended background agents. | Module 11 — the hands layer: sandboxing and the human-in-the-loop approval this module makes durable. | Temporal docs — workflows, activities, signals, and workflow versioning; the OpenAI Agents SDK Temporal integration. | LangGraph — persistence/checkpointing and time-travel; LangGraph Platform for deployment. Also Inngest and Restate for durable functions. | Anthropic — Managed Agents (create Agent → Session → stream events; scheduled cron deployments; self-hosted sandboxes); sandbox vendors E2B, Modal, Daytona, Firecracker. | . → Next: Module 13 — Frontier & Advanced Patterns .

224.title: Module 13 — Frontier & Advanced Patterns
224.content: You have built an agent (Modules 1–6), evaluated it (Module 8), instrumented it (Module 9), made it reliable and cheap (Module 10), secured it (Module 11), and given it durable execution (Module 12). You can ship the thing. This module is the one that goes stale fastest, and that is exactly why it exists: the field is moving, and the most valuable skill you can leave this course with is a map — a way to read the frontier so you can tell which new capability is real, which is demo-ware, and which of your hard-won harness code is about to be deleted by the next model. The honest framing up front: most of what gets called “the frontier” in agents right now is one of two things. Either it is a genuine capability shift — agents completing longer tasks, models trained against their own tools — or it is a packaging shift: the same inner loop from Module 3, wrapped in a new product surface (a standing identity, a cron schedule, an outer restart loop) and given a more ambitious name. Both matter. But they fail differently, and conflating them is how teams ship a “digital employee” that demos beautifully and drifts into confidently doing the wrong thing for six hours overnight. This module is about telling them apart.

225.title: Learning objectives
225.content: By the end of this module you will be able to: . | Distinguish the three things people mean by “long-running agent” — long-horizon reasoning, long-running execution, and persistent agency — and reason about each separately. | Explain the outer loop and the “Ralph Wiggum” technique, why the dumbest version of it accidentally gets the architecture right, and what “loop engineering” makes you design explicitly. | Cite the one quantitative capability trend worth anchoring on (METR’s task-length doubling) and state its honest caveat. | Predict which parts of your harness will appreciate and which will depreciate as models improve, and invest accordingly. | Place computer use and MCP correctly in your toolbox — what each is for, and where each is still brittle. | Name the binding constraints on long-running agents (verification, drift, the human-inspection problem) and explain why they are harder than raw capability. | .

226.title: 1. From task to role: the three senses of “long-running”
226.content: The phrase “long-running agent” is doing too much work. It bundles three different engineering problems that happen to co-occur, and you cannot design well until you split them: . | Long-horizon reasoning — one big task that requires many coherent steps. “Migrate this service from REST to gRPC.” The hard part is staying on-goal across hundreds of model turns without losing the thread. This is a model-capability problem, and it is the one METR measures (§3). | Long-running execution — the operational problem of staying alive: the process survives restarts, resumes after a crash, doesn’t lose state when a tool call hangs for an hour. This is durable execution — Module 12 — and it is solved infrastructure (initializer/worker patterns, hosted loops, checkpointing). It is plumbing, and good plumbing. | Persistent agency — a standing identity with accumulated memory and an open-ended charter, operating across many sessions over days and weeks. Not “do this task” but “be the on-call triage agent.” This is the “AI employee” / “digital worker” framing: a company gives an agent a name, credentials, a permission scope, and a human manager, and lets work arrive at it over time. | . Most of the breathless writing is about (3), but (3) is mostly built out of (1) and (2). An honest read is that persistent agency today is partly aspirational — the demos are real, the production deployments are narrow, and the gap between them is the subject of §7. What is actually architecturally new . If you strip the marketing, persistent agency changes three concrete things about how you build: . Work arrives over time. A task agent is a function: input → trajectory → output → exit. A role agent is a service. It mostly sits blocked on the outside world — a new ticket, a scheduled tick, a webhook — and wakes to handle an event. The LLM is no longer “the program”; it is the handler logic the service invokes when an event arrives. This is the most useful reframe in the whole module: a persistent agent is an event-driven service where an LLM decides the handler body. Everything you know about event-driven services — idempotency, queues, backpressure, dead-letter handling — applies directly and is mostly absent from “agent” tutorials. The human moves from the loop to the exception path. In an interactive agent (Module 3), a human is in the loop on every turn. In a role agent, the human is out of the loop by design — the whole point is unattended operation — and only re-enters on an exception: the agent escalates because it is stuck, hit a confirmation gate (Module 11’s blast-radius controls), or tripped a drift detector. Designing the exception path well is now the high-leverage work, because it is the only place a human can correct a run before damage compounds. Continuity lives in durable state, not context. A conversation’s continuity lives in its context window. A role agent outlives any single context window — it gets compacted (Module 4), restarted, run fresh.
