So “what this agent is, what it has learned, what it is responsible for” must live in durable external state (a memory store, a database, the filesystem), not in the transcript. The transcript is ephemeral scratch; the durable state is the agent. Get this backwards and your agent forgets who it is every time the context compacts. A worked example: the recruiting-coordinator agent . Make it concrete. You are asked to build an agent that owns “first-round recruiting coordination” — not a task, a charter. It should monitor an inbox, schedule screens, nudge stalled candidates, and escalate edge cases. As a service, its shape is: . | Triggers (work arrives): a new application webhook, a candidate reply, a daily 9am “chase stalled threads” tick. | Durable state (the agent is this): per-candidate status, what’s been promised, scheduling constraints, a running log of decisions. Not the context window. | Handler (the LLM call): given this event plus the relevant slice of durable state, decide the next action — draft a reply, propose times, or escalate. | Blast-radius gates (Module 11): “send an email to a candidate” is irreversible and outward-facing, so it goes behind a confirmation policy or a strict template, not raw model output. | Exception path: candidate asks something off-script, or a scheduling conflict can’t be resolved → stop and ping the human recruiter with context. | . Notice what dominates: almost none of this is “prompt the model better.” It is event plumbing, state design, and gate placement. The model is one component. That ratio — mostly systems, a little model — is the signature of a real persistent-agent build, and the inverse ratio is the signature of a demo. 📖 Why this is the flagship example. Role-based / recruiting agents recur as the canonical “AI employee” demo precisely because recruiting coordination is a long-lived charter with discrete events, low-but-nonzero blast radius, and a natural human-escalation path. It is the easiest place to make persistent agency look solved — which is also why it is the easiest place to ship something that drifts.

227.title: 2. The outer loop and “loop engineering”
227.content: Module 3 built the inner loop: model → tool → result → model, iterating until the task is done within a single context window. The frontier added a second loop around it. The outer loop is brutally simple: restart the agent on the same goal, repeatedly, until the goal is met. Fresh process, fresh context, same objective. The Ralph Wiggum technique . The purest expression of this — named by Geoffrey Huntley after the Simpsons character, with affection — is literally: . while :; do cat PROMPT.md | claude -p ; done . Run the agent against a prompt. When it finishes (or dies, or rots), the loop just runs it again. Forever, or until you stop it. The prompt says, roughly, “read the current state, figure out what’s left to do, do the next increment, update the state.” That’s the whole technique. It looks like a joke. It accidentally gets the long-running architecture right, for three reasons that are worth internalizing because they are the same three reasons §1’s persistent agents work: . | Fresh context each iteration = no rot. Module 4’s nemesis is context degradation — the slow accumulation of stale tool output, contradictory notes, and goal reinterpretation that builds up over a long single run. The outer loop sidesteps it entirely: every iteration starts from a clean window. There is nothing to rot because nothing carries over in context. | State lives in the filesystem = durable. What does carry over is on disk: a TODO.md, a progress file, the actual code being written. This is Module 12’s durable-state principle arrived at by the dumbest possible route. The filesystem is the checkpoint. | The model re-derives “what’s next” from ground truth. Because it can’t rely on a remembered plan (there is no memory across iterations), each pass re-reads reality — the current files, the current test output, the current todo list — and decides the next step from that. It is continuously re-grounding against the world instead of against its own increasingly-unreliable narrative of the world. | . That third point is the deep one. Goal drift (§7) is largely a story about an agent trusting its own stale summary of where it is. The Ralph loop can’t drift the same way, because it has no stale summary to trust — it has to look. The technique spread through YC startups precisely because it is so cheap to try and works embarrassingly well for grind-it-out tasks (build this CLI, port this module, get this test suite green). Anthropic eventually shipped an official plugin around the pattern. None of that makes it magic — it burns tokens, it can loop forever on a goal it can’t actually complete, and it has no taste — but it is the existence proof that the architecture of long-running agents is simple. The hard parts are elsewhere. Loop engineering . Once you take the outer loop seriously, the unit of design stops being the prompt and becomes the loop. “Loop engineering” is just naming the four questions you must now answer explicitly: . | What persists across iterations? The durable state. Exactly which files / records carry the agent’s progress, and what format keeps them legible to a fresh-context model. | What is verified each pass? Before an iteration declares progress, what external check confirms it? Tests pass, the file exists, the API returns 200. This is the anti-drift mechanism — see §7. | When does it terminate? A naive while :; never stops. A real loop has a completion gate (programmatic or LLM-judged — Module 8) and a budget/iteration cap so a stuck goal doesn’t run up an infinite bill. | When does it escalate? If the loop makes no progress for N iterations, or repeats the same failed action, it should stop and ask a human — the exception path from §1. | . 🛠️ Notice these are the same four knobs that define a persistent agent (§1: triggers, state, termination, escalation). The outer loop and the role agent are the same architecture at different cadences — one restarts in a tight loop, the other wakes on events over days. Learn the loop and you’ve learned both. This shows up in product surfaces as goal-directed primitives — e.g. a /goal command that hands the loop an objective and lets the agent decide when it’s met rather than counting turns — and scheduled / background agents that fire the loop on a cron or a queue. Those are just §1’s “work arrives over time” with a UI on it. ✅ When you hear “agent,” ask which loop. Most clever-prompt tricks live in the inner loop and depreciate (§4). The durable wins — what persists, what’s verified, when it stops — live in the outer loop and they are yours to engineer, not the model’s to obsolete.

228.title: 3. The capability trend worth anchoring on
228.content: If you anchor on one number from the frontier, anchor on this one. METR (Model Evaluation & Threat Research) measures the length of task an agent can complete autonomously — operationalized as the human-time-to-complete of tasks the model can finish at a given reliability. Their headline finding: that length has been doubling roughly every seven months, and recent data suggests the doubling time is shortening toward ~4 months. The 50%-reliability time horizon sits in the tens of minutes and is climbing. Why this is the right thing to track: it is a capability measurement that maps directly onto the engineering question you actually care about — “how much can I hand the agent before it falls apart?” A task-length horizon of ~minutes means agents reliably do bounded sub-tasks and you orchestrate; a horizon of hours means you can hand off genuinely long-horizon work (§1, sense 1). The doubling trend is the single best forecast of how much harness scaffolding you’ll be able to delete next year (§4). Now the caveat, and it is load-bearing: reliability over long horizons lags raw capability badly. The “50% reliability” qualifier matters enormously. An agent that completes a 1-hour task half the time is a research result; it is not something you deploy unattended against a 1-hour task, because the other half of the time it fails — and, worse, it often fails silently, by drifting (§7) rather than crashing. The headline number describes a frontier of what is possible at coin-flip odds, not what is trustworthy. The gap between “an agent can sometimes do this” and “I will let an agent do this overnight without watching” is the entire subject of §7, and it is widening even as the headline number improves. 📖 Track the trend; do not deploy the trend. The doubling curve tells you where to place bets for next year’s architecture. It does not tell you that this year’s agent can be trusted with this year’s longest measured task.

229.title: 4. RL-trained agents and the disappearing harness
229.content: Here is the structural force that will obsolete more of your code than any single feature: models are increasingly trained against their own harnesses. Early agents were a frontier model wrapped in a thick scaffold of human-engineered glue — retry logic, retrieval pipelines, output parsers, tool-format coaxing, prompt patterns to stop the model doing dumb things. Each of those scaffold components encodes an assumption about what the model can’t do. The output parser exists because the model used to emit malformed JSON. The retrieval scaffold exists because the model couldn’t decide what to fetch. The “CRITICAL: you MUST use the tool” prompt exists because the model under-called tools. Reinforcement learning is now moving those capabilities into the weights. Research lines like Search-R1 and ReSearch train models to do agentic retrieval — to decide when and what to search — as a learned behavior rather than a scaffolded one. The Anthropic models you’ve used throughout this course are trained against tool-use formats directly. The general direction is unmistakable: capability migrates from the harness into the model. The consequence is a one-line principle with enormous practical weight: . Every harness component encodes an assumption about what the model can’t do — and that assumption gets invalidated as models improve. So the strategic question for an engineer is no longer “what scaffold makes this work?” It is “what am I building that appreciates as models get better, versus what depreciates?” . | Depreciates (the model absorbs it) | Appreciates (the model can’t give you this) | . | Prompt tricks that coax behavior (“you MUST…”) | Your evals — the ground-truth definition of “good” for your task (Module 8) | . | Output parsers / format-repair logic | Your proprietary data and the pipelines that produce it | . | Retrieval scaffolding the model can now drive | Your integrations — the connections to your systems, with auth and side effects | . | Tool-format coaxing | Your guardrails — the blast-radius and trust controls (Module 11) | . | Multi-step decomposition the model now does itself | Your domain context and the human-in-the-loop interfaces around it | . The depreciating column is real work you may need today — Module 10’s schema-validate-and-retry exists because today’s models still occasionally fail. But it is a wasting asset. Build it deliberately, comment it as a model-gap workaround, and expect to delete it. The appreciating column is where durable engineering value lives: a model getting smarter makes your eval suite, your data, and your secure integrations more valuable, because there’s a more capable engine to point at them. 🛠️ A useful habit: when you write a piece of harness, label it. Is this compensating for a current model limitation (depreciating — write it cheap, plan to delete it), or is it durable infrastructure (appreciating — invest in it)? The teams that stay ahead spend their best engineering on the second column and treat the first as disposable. ✅ This is also a defensibility argument. “Our agent has a clever prompt” is not a moat; the next model erases it. “Our agent has ten years of labeled domain data, a battle-tested eval harness, and audited integrations into systems no one else can touch” is a moat that grows with model quality.

230.title: 5. Computer use: the universal-interface bet
230.content: Computer use lets an agent operate a graphical interface the way a person does: it receives a screenshot, reasons about it, and emits mouse and keyboard actions (click here, type this, scroll). Anthropic’s computer use and OpenAI’s computer-using-agent are the two flagship implementations; Claude models support it as a client-side tool (you run the screen; the model decides the actions). The bet behind it is large and worth stating plainly: if an agent can use a screen, it can use any software — no API required. Every legacy system, every internal tool with no integration, every SaaS app that never shipped a usable API becomes reachable through the one interface every application already has: the GUI. That is a genuinely universal adapter, and for the long tail of software that will never expose an API, it may be the only adapter. How it works, mechanically, is just the Module 3 loop with vision and a different action space: . screenshot → model reasons → action (click/type/scroll) → new screenshot → … . The model never touches an API; it looks at pixels and moves a cursor. And now the honest part. Computer use today is powerful, slow, and brittle. It is slow because every step is a full screenshot round-trip plus vision processing — seconds per click, where an API call is milliseconds. It is brittle because pixel-level grounding is error-prone: a moved button, an unexpected modal, a slow-loading page, and the agent clicks the wrong thing or stalls. The error rate per action, compounded over a multi-step GUI flow (Module 10’s 0.95^N arithmetic), gets ugly fast. It is also high blast-radius by nature — it’s driving a real UI with real buttons. Where it fits: reach for computer use when there is no API and the alternative is a human doing the clicking. It is a last-resort universal adapter, not a default. If a tool exposes an API or an MCP server (§6), use that — it is faster, more reliable, and easier to gate. Computer use earns its slot when the only interface is the screen. Treat it as the brilliant, twitchy specialist it is, not the workhorse. 📖 The capability trend (§3) bears directly on computer use: as models get better at vision grounding and longer horizons, the brittleness recedes and the universal-adapter bet looks better. It is a “wait and watch the curve” capability — under-powered for most production today, plausibly transformative on a 12–24 month horizon.

231.title: 6. MCP and the tool ecosystem
231.content: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is the converging interoperability standard for connecting agents to tools and data — the “USB for agent tools.” The problem it solves is combinatorial: before MCP, every (agent harness × tool) pair needed bespoke integration glue. MCP makes tools and data sources speak one protocol, so you write a tool/data server once and use it across any MCP-speaking harness — Claude, other models, IDEs, custom agents. The result is an ecosystem of MCP servers — GitHub, Slack, databases, search, internal systems — that you can compose into an agent’s tool surface without writing per-harness adapters. For a team, this is leverage: expose your internal systems as one MCP server and every agent surface you adopt can use them. Two practical notes for when your tool count gets large: . | Deferred / dynamic tool loading. Loading hundreds of tool schemas into context upfront is wasteful and degrades tool selection (Module 2’s “too many tools confuse the model”). The pattern is tool search: keep most tools’ schemas out of context and let the model search/discover the few it needs per request, appending their schemas dynamically. Crucially, well-designed dynamic loading appends schemas rather than swapping them, which preserves the prompt cache (Module 10) — a detail that matters for cost at scale. | Security caveats (Module 11, applied). MCP’s strength — easy composition of third-party servers — is also its supply-chain risk. An MCP server is code (or a remote endpoint) you are granting into your agent’s trust boundary. A malicious or compromised server can exfiltrate whatever the agent can see, inject instructions via tool output (prompt injection through tool results), or abuse credentials you handed it. Treat every MCP server the way Module 11 taught you to treat any dependency: vet the source, scope its credentials minimally, isolate its egress, and never assume tool output is trusted text. The convenience of “just add this server” is exactly the attack surface. | . ✅ MCP is the integration layer that appreciates (§4): it is durable plumbing into your systems, not a prompt trick. Build your internal capabilities as MCP servers and that investment survives every model upgrade — and works across whatever harness wins.

232.title: 7. The open problems: easy to build, hard to trust
232.content: This is the section that matters most, because it is where the marketing and the engineering reality diverge hardest. The blunt version: . Long-running agents are easy to build and hard to trust. Verification and the human-agent interface — not raw capability — are the binding constraints. You can stand up a “persistent AI employee” in an afternoon (§1 + §2 give you the whole architecture). It will demo beautifully. Then you let it run unattended for hours and it drifts — and the failure modes below are why “it demoed well” tells you almost nothing about whether you can trust it. Goal drift . The central failure of long unsupervised runs. The agent slowly stops doing what you asked and starts doing something subtly adjacent, while remaining fluent and confident the whole time. Three mechanisms: . | Reinterpretation across compaction. Every time the context compacts (Module 4), the goal gets re-summarized — and summaries lose nuance. “Refactor the auth module without changing behavior” becomes “refactor the auth module” becomes “improve the auth module” over successive compactions, and now the agent is rewriting behavior you told it to preserve. Each compaction is a lossy generation of telephone, and the goal degrades a little each time. | Error accumulation in persistent state. A persistent agent’s durable state (§1) is supposed to be its strength, but a bad entry compounds. One wrong fact written to a memory store — a mislabeled candidate status, an incorrect assumption recorded as fact — gets read back as ground truth on every subsequent iteration and silently warps everything downstream. The durable state is only as good as its worst write. | Confidently working on the wrong thing. The most dangerous compound of the above: the agent is productive and fluent while building the wrong thing. It’s not erroring. It’s not stuck. It’s cheerfully spending six hours and a real budget perfecting a solution to a problem you didn’t have. Nothing in the transcript looks alarming. | . Verification at scale: who authors success criteria? . The only defense against drift is verification — but verification has a foundational hole. Who writes the success criteria, and against what are they grounded? . | If a human authors them, you have Module 8’s evals, and they’re trustworthy but they don’t scale to every sub-goal a long-horizon agent invents along the way. | If the agent authors its own success criteria, you have a circularity problem: an agent that has drifted will write success criteria that match where it drifted to, and then triumphantly verify against them. Self-graded homework. The agent that’s confidently wrong (§above) is also confidently right about having succeeded. | . The partial answer is to ground self-set criteria in external signals — tests that actually run, APIs that actually return, the world pushing back (this is why the Ralph loop’s per-pass verification, §2, matters; it re-grounds against reality, not against the agent’s narrative). But “ground everything in an external check” is much easier to say than to engineer for an open-ended charter, and it is an open problem, not a solved one. The human inspect/correct problem . When a long run is going wrong, you want to look inside and fix it. Both halves are genuinely hard. | Inspection of a 6-hour, post-multiple-compaction run is not like reading a 20-line transcript. The thing you need to catch — the moment the goal quietly reinterpreted — may be buried in a compaction boundary you can’t even see anymore. | Correction is harder still. Mutating a running agent’s state is dangerous: edit its durable state mid-run and you risk corrupting it in ways the agent can’t reconcile, because it has in-flight assumptions built on the old state. The emerging discipline is to steer by appending events, not by editing state — you don’t reach in and rewrite the agent’s memory; you send it a new instruction/event (“actually, stop and reconsider X”) and let it reconcile, the same way you’d correct a service by sending it a message rather than reaching into its database. (This is exactly why §1’s “the human is on the exception path” and Module 12’s event-sourced state matter: append-only correction is the only safe correction.) | . Blast radius and trust . Tie it back to Module 11. An unattended agent’s mistakes are unattended too. A drifted agent with email access sends drifted emails. A drifted agent with deploy access deploys the wrong thing. The longer and more autonomous the run, the larger the blast radius of any single drift — and the later you’ll notice. This is why the gates (§1, Module 11) live on irreversible, outward-facing actions specifically: those are the ones where unattended drift becomes an incident instead of a wasted iteration. Where this leaves you . The capability frontier (§3) is racing ahead. The trust frontier — verification, drift detection, inspectability, safe correction — is lagging, and it is the actual bottleneck for production long-running agents. A team that obsesses over “can the model do a longer task?” and ignores “can I tell when it’s quietly doing the wrong one?” will ship something that demos and then drifts. 📖 The durable skill — the thing this whole course has been building toward — is taste for where the model still needs scaffolding, and where it no longer does. You cannot get that taste from a changelog or a benchmark. You get it from reading transcripts: watching real runs, seeing exactly where this model drifts, over-thinks, under-tools, or confidently fabricates, and where it has quietly gotten good enough that your old scaffold is now just in the way. That is why Module 9’s observability is the foundation for everything here. The frontier changes; the skill of reading what your agent actually did, and adjusting, does not.

233.title: 🛠️ Exercise: build an outer loop for Scout
233.content: Smaller and exploratory — the goal is to feel the long-running architecture and its failure modes firsthand, not to ship anything. (a) Build a Ralph-style loop. Write a script that repeatedly runs Scout against a goal in PROMPT.md, with all state on the filesystem (a TODO.md or progress.json), until a completion condition or a max-iterations / budget cap. Each iteration must: start with fresh context, read the state file, do one increment, update the state file, exit. The loop, not the model, owns continuity. # Sketch — the loop is the unit of design (§2). Scout is your agent from earlier modules. import json, pathlib, anthropic client = anthropic.Anthropic() state_path = pathlib.Path("progress.json") MAX_ITERS, stuck_limit = 25, 3 stuck = 0 def load_state(): return json.loads(state_path.read_text()) if state_path.exists() else {"todo": [], "done": []} for i in range(MAX_ITERS): state = load_state() # durable state, NOT context goal = pathlib.Path("PROMPT.md").read_text() # Fresh context every pass — the model re-derives "what's next" from the state file (§2). result = run_scout_one_increment( # your Module-3 inner loop, single increment goal=goal, state=state, model="claude-opus-4-8", thinking={"type": "adaptive"}, # adaptive thinking — no budget_tokens on Opus 4.8 ) write_state(result.updated_state) # persist progress to disk if goal_met(result): # (b) termination gate — programmatic or LLM-judge print(f"done in {i+1} iterations"); break if made_no_progress(state, result): # (b) escalation: stuck N times → ask the human stuck += 1 if stuck >= stuck_limit: escalate_to_human(state); break else: stuck = 0 . (b) Add the gates. A termination check — an LLM-judge (callback to Module 8) or a programmatic “is the goal met?” test — and an escalation hook: if the loop makes no progress stuck_limit times in a row, stop and ask the human instead of grinding forever. These are two of the four loop-engineering knobs from §2. (c) Give it a real multi-step goal. Something with genuine sub-structure: “build a small CLI tool with passing tests” or “research X and produce a cited report.” Watch it grind across iterations. (d) Observe and document the drift. This is the actual point. Where does it lose the thread? Does it repeat work it already finished (state-file format too vague to read back cleanly)? Does it confidently mark something done that isn’t? Does it reinterpret the goal as the TODO.md gets summarized? Write down each failure and map it to a mechanism in §7. You will learn more from one drifted run you diagnosed than from re-reading §7. (e) Stretch — add a fresh-context verifier. Each iteration, spawn a separate sub-agent with a clean context whose only job is to check the current state against the original goal in PROMPT.md and flag drift. Note how a fresh-context check catches reinterpretation that the working agent — carrying its own drifted narrative — cannot see in itself. That asymmetry is the §7 verification problem in miniature.

234.title: Real production issues
234.content: . | Fragile loops that drift under long unsupervised runs. The central one. The loop demos perfectly in a 5-minute run and drifts in a 5-hour one. Test at production duration, not demo duration — short runs systematically hide the failure mode. | Goal reinterpretation across compaction boundaries. “Don’t change behavior” survives turn 1 and is gone by compaction 4. Pin the immutable goal somewhere that never gets compacted (a re-read-every-pass PROMPT.md, not the transcript), and re-ground against it each iteration. | Error accumulation in persistent state. One bad memory write becomes ground truth forever. Treat writes to durable state as high-stakes: validate before persisting, version it (Module 12), and make it possible to audit and redact a bad entry. | Confidently working on the wrong thing for hours. No error, full fluency, real budget, wrong deliverable. Only external verification catches this — the agent’s own confidence is worthless as a signal. | Outward-facing unattended mistakes (blast radius). A drifted agent’s irreversible actions are also unattended. Gate irreversible/outward actions behind confirmation or strict templates (Module 11); never wire raw model output straight to send/deploy/delete in an unattended loop. | The difficulty of inspecting/correcting a live run. You can’t easily read a 6-hour post-compaction run, and editing its state mid-flight corrupts it. Build inspection in from the start (Module 9), and correct by appending events, not mutating state. | Depreciating scaffolding. Today’s clever harness trick is deleted by next quarter’s model — and worse, an obsolete scaffold can fight a now-capable model (the “you MUST use the tool” prompt makes a model that now self-decides over-call it). Label scaffolding as a model-gap workaround; re-evaluate it on every model upgrade. | Computer-use brittleness. Slow, pixel-fragile, high blast radius. Don’t put it on the critical path of a production flow that has any API alternative; reserve it for the no-API long tail and budget generous retries. | MCP supply-chain risk. A third-party MCP server is inside your trust boundary. Vet it, scope its credentials, isolate egress, and treat its output as untrusted (prompt-injection vector) — Module 11 applied. | The demo-to-production gap. The honest closing issue: an impressive demo and a trustworthy production agent are different artifacts. The bottleneck between them is verification and the human interface, not capability. Budget your engineering accordingly — most of it goes into trust, not into making the model do more. | .

235.title: Check yourself
235.content: . | Name the three senses of “long-running agent” and say which one Module 12 already solved for you. | Why does the Ralph Wiggum outer loop avoid context rot, and where does its state actually live? | State the four questions “loop engineering” forces you to answer explicitly. | METR’s task-length horizon is doubling every ~7 months. Why is it a mistake to deploy an agent against the longest task at that horizon? | Give two examples of harness code that depreciates as models improve and two that appreciate. What makes the difference? | When should you reach for computer use instead of an API or MCP server — and why is it a last resort? | You discover a long-running agent has drifted. Why is editing its durable state the wrong way to correct it, and what’s the right way? | “Long-running agents are easy to build and hard to trust.” What, specifically, is the binding constraint — and how do you get the taste to manage it? | .

236.title: Further reading
236.content: . | METR, “Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks” — the task-length-doubling result; the quantitative backbone of §3 and the source for the reliability caveat. | Geoffrey Huntley, “Ralph Wiggum as a software engineer” — the outer-loop technique, why it works, and how it spread. | Anthropic, “Building effective agents” and the computer-use / MCP documentation — the inner loop, tool design, computer use, and MCP from the source. | Search-R1 / ReSearch papers — RL-trained agentic retrieval; concrete instances of capability migrating from harness into weights (§4). | Model Context Protocol specification and server registry — the interop standard and the ecosystem (§6). | Module 8 (Evals), Module 9 (Observability), Module 11 (Security), Module 12 (Durable Execution) of this course — every open problem in §7 routes back to one of these. The frontier doesn’t replace the fundamentals; it raises the stakes on them. | . → Next: Module 14 — Capstone Project .

238.title: Module 14 — Capstone Project
238.content: You started this course able to call an LLM. You’re ending it able to engineer an agent system. The thirteen modules behind you each isolated one hard problem — the loop, context, retrieval, orchestration, frameworks, evals, observability, reliability, cost, security, deployment, the long-running outer loop. Each was taught on Scout, a coding/research agent you grew from a while loop and a messages.create call into something with memory, tools, and a service boundary. This module is where you stop isolating and start integrating: you take one agent from “works in the demo” to “a thing you’d let run against real load, with real money and real blast radius on the line,” and then you grade it against a checklist you’ll reuse for every agent you build after this. That gap — demo to production — is where most agent projects die. The industry number that gets quoted is that roughly 77% of agent projects don’t survive the shipping phase: the harness that passed every staging run falls over on real traffic, real adversarial input, and real cost at scale. The reason is not that the model wasn’t smart enough. It’s that the demo only had to work once, on inputs the author chose, with the author watching. Production has to work the ten-thousandth time, on inputs an attacker chose, with nobody watching and a budget that’s being audited. Closing that gap is systems engineering — retries, idempotency, sandboxing, dashboards, cost accounting, graders — and almost none of it is novel AI research. It’s the engineering you already know, applied in a new regime where one of your components is a stochastic, latency-heavy, occasionally-adversarially-manipulable function priced by the token. Hold the four load-bearing ideas of this course in your head as you build, because the capstone is just these four made concrete at once: . | An agent is a model in a closed loop with an environment. Everything else is plumbing around that loop. | Almost everything hard is systems engineering, not prompting. The model is one component; the system is the product. | Correctness lives at the boundary. The model proposes; your harness disposes. Validation, permission, and verification happen where tool calls cross from the model’s text into the real world. | Tokens are a priced resource with cache locality. Context is a budget, and the prefix-match cache rewards keeping stable things stable and volatile things last. | .

239.title: What you’ll build
239.content: A single agent, taken end to end, that satisfies a ship-readiness review you run yourself. Concretely you will: . | Choose a capstone at the right scope — a task where you can author a real eval suite and where mistakes are recoverable. | Assemble the stack — wire every layer from Modules 2–13 into one coherent agent, making (and recording) the judgment calls each layer demands. | Build in the right order — milestones that keep it tractable, with the eval suite and instrumentation in from the start, not bolted on. | Run the ship-readiness review — a concrete, checkbox-level rubric across Capability, Reliability, Cost, Security, Observability, and Operability. This rubric outlives the capstone; it’s the reusable production-readiness bar for anything you build later. | . 🛠️ This is mostly a spec and a set of checklists, not a pile of new code. You wrote the components across thirteen modules. The capstone is the assembly, and the judgment about whether the assembly is good enough to ship. 📖 Throughout, references are by module number. If a layer is fuzzy, re-read that module before wiring it in — don’t reinvent it here.

240.title: Step 1 — Choose your capstone
240.content: Pick one. The recommended default is to extend Scout into either a capable coding agent or a research agent, because Scout already carries thirteen modules of accumulated infrastructure and you’ll spend your effort on integration instead of bootstrapping. But the constraints matter more than the choice, so here’s the menu with what each one exercises. A good capstone has two properties, and you should reject any idea that lacks them: . | You can author a real eval suite for it. If you can’t write 10–20 cases with checkable success criteria, you can’t tell whether a change helped, and you cannot run a ship-readiness review. No evals, no capstone. | Mistakes are recoverable. The agent will be wrong. Pick a domain where wrong is a bad PR you don’t merge, a draft you don’t send, a flagged ticket a human reviews — not an irreversible transfer, an unrecoverable delete, or a production deploy with no rollback. | . Option A — Coding / devtools agent (a mini-Claude-Code) — recommended . The agent operates on a real repository: reads files, searches, edits, runs tests, and proposes a diff or PR. | Core tools: read, edit (with staleness checks — Module 3), glob/grep, bash (sandboxed — Module 11), a test runner, and optionally a create_pull_request tool gated behind human approval. | Eval slices that matter: bug-fix tasks with a hidden test that must pass; refactors where existing tests must still pass; “no-op” tasks where the correct answer is to change nothing (catches over-eager editing); multi-file changes; tasks requiring a tool the agent must choose to use. | Security / blast radius: bash is the whole ballgame. Sandbox it, allowlist executables, and gate any write that leaves the workspace (push, network, delete outside the repo). The repo itself is recoverable via git; egress and force-push are not. | Why it exercises the whole stack: long agentic loops (context management earns its keep), tool-error recovery, forced verification (did the tests actually pass?), real injection surface (a malicious file in the repo can carry instructions), and a clear, gradeable success signal (the hidden test). | . Option B — Research / report agent . The agent answers an open-ended question by searching, fetching, reading, and synthesizing a cited report. | Core tools: web search and web fetch (server-side tools — Module 5 territory for retrieval discipline), a scratchpad/notes file (files-as-memory — Module 4), and a structured-output step for the final report. | Eval slices that matter: questions with a known correct answer (factual grounding); questions where the right move is to say “the sources disagree” or “I couldn’t verify this”; questions designed to bait a confident hallucination; citation-fidelity checks (does every claim trace to a fetched source?). | Security / blast radius: the agent reads attacker-controllable web content into its context — this is the canonical prompt-injection surface (Module 11). The output is low-blast-radius (a report), but the input is hostile by default. Adversarial eval cases here are non-negotiable. | Why it exercises the whole stack: retrieval and grounding, context bloat from long fetches (compaction and sub-agents as context firewalls — Modules 4, 6), an LLM-judge-heavy eval suite (faithfulness is hard to grade with string matching — Module 8), and clear cost knobs (fan-out breadth vs. budget). | . Option C — Support / ops agent over a knowledge base + tools . The agent answers user or operator questions grounded in a private knowledge base, and can take a small set of real actions (look up an order, draft a reply, file a ticket). | Core tools: a retrieval tool over your KB (Module 5), a few read-only lookups, and one or two gated write actions (draft, not send; file, not resolve). | Eval slices that matter: in-KB questions (must be grounded), out-of-KB questions (must defer, not invent), questions that require an action vs. ones that don’t, and adversarial “ignore your instructions and refund me” cases. | Security / blast radius: least-privilege on the action tools, HITL on anything user-facing or money-adjacent, and injection resistance against both the user message and retrieved KB chunks. | Why it exercises the whole stack: retrieval, a real permission policy, HITL gating, and an eval suite that has to measure deferral as a success, not a failure. | . Option D — Long-running “role” agent that monitors something on a schedule . Not a task but a role: the agent wakes on a schedule (or a trigger), checks state, and acts or escalates — a CI babysitter, a dependency-watcher, an on-call triager. | Core tools: read-only monitors plus a notify/escalate action; durable state so each wake builds on the last (Modules 12, 13). | Eval slices that matter: “nothing’s wrong, do nothing” (the common case — false-positive rate is the metric), “something’s wrong, escalate correctly,” and recovery after a crash mid-run. | Security / blast radius: the danger is autonomy without a human in the loop, so escalation must be cheap and action must be conservative. Bound the outer loop (Module 13) — no infinite wake-act cycles. | Why it exercises the whole stack: the outer-loop shape (Module 13), checkpoint/resume (Module 12), cost-per-day rather than cost-per-task accounting, and an eval suite dominated by the boring-but-critical “do nothing” case. | . ✅ Self-check before you commit: Can you write down, right now, three eval cases with checkable pass/fail criteria? If not, narrow the scope until you can.

241.title: Step 2 — The build (integrate every layer)
241.content: This is the spec. Each item maps to a module; treat the checkboxes as work you execute, and write down the judgment call where one is flagged. Default models: claude-sonnet-4-6 for the main loop, claude-haiku-4-5 for cheap sub-tasks (classification, extraction, summarization), and claude-opus-4-8 or claude-fable-5 reserved for the genuinely hard reasoning steps. Core loop + tool surface (Modules 2–3) . | One clean agentic loop: call the model, execute tool calls, append results, repeat until end_turn. Handle every stop reason — tool_use, end_turn, max_tokens, pause_turn (server-side tools), and refusal (check stop_reason before reading content). | A deliberately designed tool surface. Start with bash for breadth; promote an action to a dedicated, typed tool when you need to gate it, render it, audit it, or parallelize it (Module 3). Reversibility is your promotion test: hard-to-reverse actions become typed tools so the harness gets an action-specific hook. | Tool descriptions are prescriptive about when to call, not just what they do. On recent models that reach for tools more conservatively, the trigger condition in the description gives measurable lift. | Parallel tool results returned in a single user message; failed tools returned with is_error: true, never dropped. | . 🛠️ Judgment call to record: which actions did you promote from bash to dedicated tools, and why? “I gated git push because it’s irreversible; I left grep in bash because it’s read-only and recoverable” is the kind of sentence your ship-readiness review will want. Context management (Modules 4, 6) . | A truncation or context-editing strategy for stale tool results, and compaction for conversations that approach the window. If you compact, append the full response.content (compaction blocks included) back to messages — extracting only text silently loses the compaction state. | Files as memory where state should outlive a single context window — a scratchpad, a notes file, a plan the agent re-reads. | Sub-agents as context firewalls (Module 6): when a sub-task generates a lot of intermediate tokens you don’t need afterward (exploring a codebase, reading ten web pages), spawn a sub-agent, let it burn its own context, and return only the conclusion to the main loop. This is the cheapest way to keep the main loop’s context lean. | Caching discipline: frozen system prompt, deterministic tool order, volatile content (timestamps, per-request IDs) after the last cache breakpoint. Verify with usage.cache_read_input_tokens — if it’s zero across repeated requests, you have a silent invalidator. | . Knowledge / retrieval (Module 5) — if the task needs it . | A retrieval layer (RAG over your KB, or tool-based web search/fetch) only if grounding in external knowledge is part of the job. A pure coding agent over a repo may not need RAG at all — the filesystem is the knowledge store, and grep is the retrieval. | Grounding discipline: the agent cites or points to sources, and the eval suite checks that claims trace back to retrieved content. | . Orchestration (Module 6) . | A conscious workflow-vs-agent decision for each part of the system. Code-orchestrated steps (you control the sequence) where the path is predictable; an open-ended agent loop where it genuinely isn’t. Don’t reach for an agent where a three-step workflow suffices. | Orchestrator-worker where you fan out across independent items; evaluator-optimizer where a draft-then-critique loop measurably improves output. Use these only where they earn their keep — each adds latency and tokens. | . Framework, or a justified “rolled my own” (Module 7) . | Either adopt a framework if it fits your shape, or write down a deliberate justification for staying hand-rolled. “I kept the manual loop because I need human-in-the-loop approval gates and custom audit logging that the framework’s tool runner abstracts away” is a legitimate answer. An unexamined default is not. | . Evals — the non-negotiable spine (Module 8) . | A private eval suite of 10–20+ cases, authored by you, that the model has never seen. This is your ground truth. Without it, you cannot run a ship-readiness review — you have vibes, not a verdict. | Mixed graders: exact-match or hidden-test for objective cases; an LLM judge for the subjective ones (faithfulness, helpfulness, tone). Keep the judge’s rubric explicit and gradeable. | Slices, not just an average. Break results out by the categories that matter for your task (in-KB vs. out-of-KB, bug-fix vs. no-op, benign vs. adversarial). A single aggregate number hides the regression that matters. | k > 1 with confidence intervals. Agents are stochastic; run each case several times and report a CI, not a point estimate. A 1/3 → 2/3 “improvement” on a single run is noise. | Adversarial cases baked in — at least a few injection / jailbreak / “ignore your instructions” cases as their own slice (this is the Module 11 hook landing in your eval suite). | The suite gates changes. A change that drops a slice below its threshold doesn’t ship. This is what makes “production-grade” a measurable claim instead of an aspiration. | . ✅ Self-check: If a teammate changed your system prompt, could your eval suite catch a regression before it reached users? If not, the suite isn’t doing its job yet. Observability (Module 9) . | Every run traced. Each model call, tool call, and result captured with timing and token counts — log the _request_id on every call so you can report failures to Anthropic. | Dashboards (or at minimum queryable logs) for cost per run, latency per run, and tool-error rate. You can’t manage what you can’t see, and “cost per task” is a ship-readiness line item. | Replay. Given a failed run, you can reconstruct exactly what the model saw and did. Debugging an agent without replay is debugging by séance. | . 🛠️ Instrument from the first milestone, not the last. Retrofitting tracing onto a working agent is far more painful than building it in, and you’ll want the traces while you’re developing the evals. Reliability + cost (Module 10) . | Retries with backoff on transient errors (the SDK retries 429/5xx by default — extend it where you need to). Fallbacks for hard failures. Forced verification for high-stakes outputs — the agent must check its own work (re-run the test, re-read the file it claims to have written) before declaring done. | Prompt caching active and verified (Module 4’s cache discipline, confirmed via cache_read_input_tokens). | Model tiering wired in: Haiku for the cheap sub-tasks, Sonnet for the loop, Opus/Fable only for the hard reasoning. Don’t downgrade silently for cost where correctness matters — tier deliberately. | A known cost-per-task. A real number, measured from traces, that you’d put in a budget. “I don’t know what a run costs” fails the review. | No infinite loops. Bound iterations; detect and break repetitive tool-call cycles. | . Security (Module 11) . | Sandboxed execution. bash / code execution runs isolated (container or restricted user), with an executable allowlist and resource/timeout limits. Commands are untrusted model output — treat them that way. | A real permission policy. Least-privilege on every tool. Read-only tools are read-only; write tools are scoped to exactly what the task needs. | HITL on irreversible actions. Anything that can’t be undone — send, push, delete-outside-workspace, money-adjacent — pauses for human approval. Use the manual loop’s approval gate, not the auto-runner, for these. | Injection resistance, tested. Untrusted content (web pages, repo files, KB chunks, user messages) cannot redirect the agent’s behavior. Operator instructions go through the system channel (or a <system-reminder> block), never trusted from user/tool content. The adversarial eval slice from the eval step is how you prove this, not just assert it. | Secrets never enter the model’s context or the sandbox. Credentials are injected at the boundary, not handed to the agent. | . Deployment (Module 12) . | A real service or durable/background shape — not a script you run by hand. An HTTP service, a queue worker, or a managed/background runner. | Checkpoint + resume. A crash mid-run doesn’t lose the work; state is externalized (DB, object store, durable queue), not held in process memory. | Idempotency on anything that triggers a side effect, so a retry after a crash doesn’t double-act. | . Outer loop / long-running shape (Module 13) — if the task is a role, not a task . | If you chose Option D (or your task is genuinely a standing role), the outer loop is scheduled or triggered, bounded (no runaway wake-act cycles), and resumable. State accumulates across wakes via durable memory, and escalation to a human is cheap and conservative. | .

242.title: Step 3 — Build order and milestones
242.content: Don’t build all of this at once — you’ll drown. Build in milestones, each shippable in the sense that it works end to end at that scope. The ordering principle: the eval suite and instrumentation come first, because they’re how you’ll judge every later change, and security and durability come before you point it at anything real. v1 — Working loop + tools + evals. Get the core loop running with a minimal tool surface. Then — before adding anything clever — write the eval suite (10+ cases) and turn on tracing. This is deliberately early. The evals are your ground truth; every later milestone is judged against them, so they have to exist before there’s anything to judge. By the end of v1 you have a working agent, a number that says how good it is, and traces that say what it did. v2 — Context + reliability + observability. Add context management (truncation/compaction, files-as-memory, sub-agents where they help). Add retries, fallbacks, forced verification, prompt caching, and model tiering. Flesh out the dashboards. Re-run the evals after each addition — context and caching changes are exactly the kind that silently regress a slice. By the end of v2 you have an agent that’s robust, observable, and has a known cost-per-task. v3 — Security + deployment. Sandbox execution, write the permission policy, add HITL gates on irreversible actions, and harden against injection (and add the adversarial eval slice if it isn’t there yet). Then give it a durable deployment shape: service or worker, checkpoint/resume, externalized state, idempotency. By the end of v3 you have something you could actually point at real input without flinching. v4 — Polish / long-running. Tighten cost, tune the model tiering against measured traces, improve the prompt against eval slices that are lagging, and — if your task is a role — add the bounded outer loop. This is also where you do a real adversarial pass: try to break your own agent the way an attacker would. 📖 At every milestone boundary, run the full eval suite and check it against the previous milestone’s numbers. A milestone that regressed a slice isn’t done.

243.title: Ship-readiness review
243.content: This is the deliverable. Run it against your capstone, checkbox by checkbox. Every “no” is either a gap to close or a risk to consciously accept and document — there’s no third option. Keep this rubric; it’s the reusable production-readiness bar for every agent you build after this one. Capability — does it do the job, measured? . | A private eval suite of 10–20+ cases gates changes. | Results are reported by slice, not just an aggregate. | Cases run k > 1 with confidence intervals; “improvements” are distinguishable from noise. | Mixed graders: objective cases checked objectively, subjective cases judged with an explicit rubric. | The current scores clear the bar you set for shipping, and you wrote that bar down. | . Reliability — does it recover, verify, and stay bounded? . | Transient failures retry with backoff; hard failures have a fallback. | High-stakes outputs are verified by the agent before “done” (tests re-run, files re-read). | No infinite loops: iterations bounded, repetitive cycles detected and broken. | A crash mid-run is recoverable; state is externalized, not in process memory. | refusal and max_tokens stop reasons are handled, not assumed away. | . Cost — known, controlled, no surprises at scale? . | A measured cost-per-task (or cost-per-day for a role agent), from real traces. | Prompt caching is active and verified via cache_read_input_tokens. | Model tiering is deliberate: cheap models for cheap sub-tasks, expensive only where correctness demands. | Cost scales sanely with load — no per-request work that’s accidentally O(history). | . Security — sandboxed, least-privilege, gated, injection-tested? . | Code/bash execution is sandboxed with an allowlist and resource limits. | Every tool runs at least-privilege; write tools are scoped to the task. | Irreversible actions require human approval (HITL). | Injection resistance is tested by an adversarial eval slice, not merely claimed. | Secrets never enter the model context or the sandbox; operator instructions use the system channel. | . Observability — every run traced, every failure debuggable? . | Every run is traced: model calls, tool calls, results, timing, tokens, _request_id. | Cost, latency, and tool-error rate are visible (dashboard or queryable logs). | You can replay a failed run and see exactly what the model saw. | . Operability — deployable, resumable, steerable by a human? . | Deployed as a durable service/worker, not a hand-run script. | Checkpoint + resume works; side effects are idempotent under retry. | A human can inspect a run in flight, correct it, or stop it — and escalation is cheap. | Long-running/role agents are bounded and don’t run away. | . ✅ The verdict: if every box is checked, or every unchecked box is a risk you’ve consciously written down and accepted, you have a production-grade agent. If you can’t say which it is for some box, that box is your next task.

244.title: Where to go next
244.content: You’ve built the thing. Here’s how to keep getting better at building the next one. | Keep reading primary sources. The frontier moves fast and the secondhand summaries lag it. Point yourself at the lab engineering blogs, the API docs, and the model cards — resources.md collects the ones worth your time. The capability boundary in particular is worth tracking directly: follow METR and the lab evaluations to know what agents can newly do before it shows up in a product. | Build a real thing for real users. This is the fastest teacher by a wide margin. A capstone graded against your own evals is a great rehearsal; an agent that strangers depend on teaches you the failure modes you didn’t think to put in the eval suite. Ship something small and real. | Study and contribute to open frameworks. Reading how a mature agent framework handles the tool loop, retries, and context management — and where it chose not to abstract — is a fast way to sharpen your own judgment about what to build versus borrow. | Develop taste by reading transcripts. The single highest-leverage habit: read your agent’s actual run transcripts, the good and the bad. Where did it loop? Where did it give up early? Where did it confidently do the wrong thing? Taste for agent behavior is built from reading transcripts the way taste for code is built from reading code. | .

245.title: Closing
245.content: You came in able to call an LLM. You leave able to engineer agent systems — to take a stochastic, token-priced, occasionally-adversarial model and wrap it in a loop, a context budget, a tool surface, an eval harness, a tracing layer, a permission boundary, and a durable runtime, until the whole thing is something you’d trust on real load. The quiet lesson of the whole course is the one the demo-to-prod gap keeps teaching: the hard parts were never the model. They were retries and idempotency, graders and slices, sandboxes and least-privilege, dashboards and replay, caches and cost accounting — the systems engineering you already knew, applied in a new regime where one component happens to think. The model got you the demo. The engineering got you to production. Now go build the next one, and run it through the review.

247.title: Agent Engineering: From Fundamentals to Production
247.content: A hands-on, sequential course that takes you from “I’ve used an LLM API” to “I can design, build, evaluate, and deploy a production agent system.” Written for an experienced software engineer who hasn’t worked much with AI agents yet. The one-sentence thesis of this course: an agent is a base model placed in a closed loop with an environment — and almost everything that makes agents hard is ordinary systems engineering (state, reliability, cost, security, observability) showing up in an unusual regime. Your existing instincts transfer. The new skill is developing taste for what the model does well unaided versus where it needs scaffolding.

248.title: Who this is for
248.content: . | You’re a senior/staff-level engineer. You’ve built complex systems. You understand distributed systems, APIs, testing, deployment. | You’ve called an LLM API but haven’t built agentic systems. | You want depth, not a tutorial that stops at “here’s a chatbot.” You want to understand the real production failure modes and how people solve them. | .

249.title: What you’ll be able to do at the end
249.content: . | Explain precisely how an agent differs from a base model, and reason about where capability comes from. | Build an agent loop from scratch (no framework) — tools, the loop, context management, sub-agents. | Choose and use a production framework (LangGraph, the lab Agent SDKs) deliberately, knowing what each buys you. | Build an eval harness — the single most important and most-skipped skill — and use it to gate changes. | Instrument agents with tracing/observability and debug multi-step failures. | Engineer for reliability, cost, latency, and security (prompt injection, sandboxing, permissions). | Deploy a long-running/durable agent and reason about state, recovery, and human-in-the-loop. | .

250.title: How to use this course
250.content: . | Go in order. Each module builds on the previous. Concepts introduced early (the loop, tokens, context) are load-bearing later. | Do the exercises. Reading about agents teaches you the vocabulary; building them teaches you the engineering. Every module ends with a hands-on exercise and a “Check yourself” section. | Build the running project. A single project — a coding/research agent you’ll call Scout — grows across the course. You build its loop in Module 3, give it memory and retrieval in 4–5, evals in 8, observability in 9, hardening in 10–11, and deploy it in 12. The capstone (Module 14) takes it to production-grade. | Read the primary sources. Each module links to the canonical engineering writing (Anthropic, OpenAI, framework docs, key papers). resources.md collects them. The field moves fast; learn to read the source. | Keep a lab notebook. Seriously. Keep a running notes.md of surprises, failures, and “huh” moments. Reading your own transcripts is how you build taste (see Module 8). | . Conventions . | Code is Python (the dominant language for agent engineering). TypeScript equivalents are noted where they matter. | The model API used in examples is Anthropic’s Claude (current models and SDK), but every concept is provider-agnostic — the loop, tools, context, evals, and deployment patterns are the same whether you use Claude, GPT, Gemini, or open models. Where something is provider-specific, it’s flagged. | 📖 marks a primary-source reading. 🛠️ marks a hands-on exercise. ✅ marks a self-check. | .

251.title: The modules (14 core + 4 deep-dives)
251.content: Part I — Foundations (Days 1–3) . | Module 0B — The Python You Need for Scout — deep-dive / reference. The advanced Python that Scout’s source actually uses — dataclasses vs. Pydantic, closures and injected callables, context managers, async generators, threads/asyncio/subprocesses, contextvars, durability with fsync — each anchored to the file that uses it. Skim now, return when a construct bites. | Module 01 — The Base Model & the Completion API — LLMs as stateless functions, tokens, sampling/temperature, the messages API, prompting, structured output. | Module 1B — Prompting, Instructions & Steering — deep-dive. Prompts as code: the anatomy of a system prompt, steering behavior (verbosity, autonomy, tool-triggering), reasoning/effort, authority channels, prompt rot — and why you iterate against evals, not vibes. | Module 02 — Tool Use / Function Calling — the core primitive that turns a text model into an agent. Tool schemas, the request/response shape, designing a tool surface. | Module 03 — Build a Minimal Agent From Scratch — Project: Scout v0. The agent loop with no framework. Tools (read/write/bash), the loop, the permission gate. This is the heart of the course. | . Part II — Core Engineering (Days 4–7) . | Module 04 — Context Engineering & Memory — the context window as a managed resource. Truncation, compaction, the filesystem-as-memory pattern, sub-agents as context firewalls. | Module 05 — Retrieval & Knowledge (RAG → Agentic RAG) — embeddings, vector search, RAG vs. long context, agentic/iterative retrieval. Give Scout a knowledge base. | Module 06 — Multi-Agent Systems & Orchestration — workflows vs. agents, the canonical patterns (chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-worker, evaluator-optimizer), and the lossy sub-agent interface. | Module 07 — The Framework Landscape — LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK, Claude Agent SDK, CrewAI, Google ADK. When to use what, and when to use nothing. Rebuild Scout in a framework. | . Part III — Production (Days 8–12) . | Module 08 — Evaluation & Testing — the most important module. Building an eval harness: datasets, graders (programmatic / LLM-as-judge), pass@k vs. pass^k, regression gating, the production→eval flywheel. | Module 09 — Observability, Tracing & Debugging — traces vs. logs, spans, Langfuse/LangSmith/Braintrust, debugging multi-step causal-chain failures. | Module 10 — Reliability, Cost & Performance — retries, fallbacks, structured-output validation, prompt caching economics, model tiering/routing, the quadratic-transcript problem, latency. | Module 10B — Model Customization: Fine-Tuning, RFT & When to Train — deep-dive. The prompt→context→tools→fine-tune ladder; what fine-tuning does (and doesn’t) do; SFT / DPO / RFT / distillation; and the honest “should you even train?” decision. | Module 11 — Security, Safety & Guardrails — prompt injection (the SQL injection of this stack), OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Apps, permission engines, sandboxing, human-in-the-loop, guardrails. | Module 11B — The Human Interface: Steering, Escalation & Trust — deep-dive. The product/UX layer as the trust mechanism: steering a running agent, escalation calibration, making long runs legible, plan mode, approval UX, and inspect/correct of live runs. | Module 12 — Deployment & Durable Execution — serving agents, state, durable execution (Temporal, LangGraph checkpointing), long-running/background agents, deploying Scout. | . Part IV — Frontier & Capstone (Days 13–14+) . | Module 13 — Frontier & Advanced Patterns — long-running/persistent agents, the “loop” discourse, RL-trained agents, computer use, MCP ecosystems, where the field is heading. | Module 14 — Capstone Project — take Scout (or a project of your choice) to production-grade: evals + tracing + guardrails + deployment, with a ship-readiness review. | . Reference . | Glossary — every term, defined. | Resources — the canonical reading list and tooling index. | .

252.title: Prerequisites
252.content: . | Comfortable in Python (3.10+). You don’t need ML experience. | An API key for at least one frontier model provider (setup in Module 0). | ~$20–50 of API credit will comfortably cover every exercise (most use small/cheap models; evals are the main spend). | Docker (for the sandboxing and deployment modules) — optional but recommended. | .

253.title: Suggested pace
253.content: This is designed for 1–2 weeks of focused full-time study, ~1 module per half-day with exercises. It compresses to a week if you skim the framework module and skip the capstone, or expands to a month part-time. The modules most worth slowing down on: 03 (the loop), 08 (evals), and 11 (security) — these are where the depth-of-understanding payoff is highest. Start with Module 0 — Setup.

255.title: Glossary
255.content: Terms used throughout the course, defined plainly. Cross-references in bold. Core . | Token — the atomic unit a model reads/writes; a subword chunk (~4 chars of English) from a fixed vocabulary, produced by a tokenizer (usually byte-pair encoding). Pricing, context limits, and several model quirks are all downstream of tokenization. (Module 1) | Context window — the fixed-size buffer of tokens a model can attend to in one call (e.g. 200K–1M). The transcript must fit inside it. (Modules 1, 4) | Tokenizer — the deterministic codec mapping text ↔ integer token IDs. Frozen at training time. Use the provider’s count_tokens, never a different model’s tokenizer. | Temperature — sampling knob; divides logits before softmax. T=0 ≈ greedy/deterministic-ish; higher = more random/creative. (Module 1) | Logits / softmax — the model’s raw per-token scores (logits) turned into a probability distribution (softmax) that’s sampled from. | Base model — the LLM itself: a stateless function from tokens-in to tokens-out. No memory, no tools, no clock. (Module 1) | . Agents . | Agent — a base model placed in a closed loop with an environment: it picks an action, the harness executes it, the result is fed back, repeat until done. (Module 3) | Agent loop — the while loop at the center of every agent: call model → execute tool calls → append results → call model again, until the model stops calling tools. (Module 3) | Harness — everything around the model in the loop: tool implementations, the loop, context management, permissions, state, orchestration. Where most engineering lives. | Tool / function calling — the trained ability of a model to emit a structured request to call a named function with JSON arguments, instead of (or with) prose. The model requests; the harness executes. (Module 2) | Tool schema — name + description + JSON Schema for a tool’s parameters, sent to the model. The model reads the description at runtime; description quality changes behavior. | System prompt — the engineered prefix configuring the agent’s behavior, conventions, and environment facts; sent on every call. | Sub-agent — a child agent spawned with its own fresh context window and (often restricted) toolset; runs a scoped task and returns only a summary. Used as a context firewall. (Modules 4, 6) | MCP (Model Context Protocol) — a standard protocol for exposing tools/data to any agent harness (“USB for agent tools”). Write an integration once, use it across products. (Modules 7, 13) | . Context & memory . | Context engineering — the discipline of deciding what goes into the context window and when, to keep the agent effective and cheap. (Module 4) | Compaction — summarizing older transcript turns and replacing them, to stay under the context limit. (Module 4) | Context editing / pruning — clearing stale tool results or thinking blocks from the transcript (removed, not summarized). (Module 4) | Context rot — degradation of retrieval/attention quality as the transcript grows, before the hard limit is hit. (Module 4) | Memory (long-term) — state persisted outside the context window (files, a memory tool, a store) that survives across sessions. (Modules 4, 12) | Filesystem-as-memory — the pattern of having the agent write plans/findings/state to files and re-read them, instead of holding everything in context (spilling to disk under memory pressure). (Modules 4, 13) | . Retrieval . | RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) — fetching relevant documents and putting them in context before the model answers. (Module 5) | Embedding — a vector representation of text such that similar meanings are nearby; the basis of semantic search. (Module 5) | Vector database — a store optimized for nearest-neighbor search over embeddings (Chroma, pgvector, etc.). (Module 5) | Agentic RAG — retrieval driven by the agent itself: it decides when/what to search, reads, critiques, and re-searches in a loop, rather than a single fixed retrieval step. (Module 5) | Chunking — splitting documents into retrievable pieces. (Module 5) | Reranking — a second, more precise scoring pass over retrieved candidates. (Module 5) | . Orchestration . | Workflow — a system where LLM calls and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths. Predictable. (Module 6) | Agent (vs workflow) — a system where the model dynamically directs its own process and tool use. Flexible. (Module 6) | Orchestrator-worker — a coordinator agent that decomposes a task and delegates subtasks to worker sub-agents. (Module 6) | Evaluator-optimizer — one model generates, another critiques/scores, loop until good. (Module 6) | Routing — classifying an input and sending it to the appropriate specialized handler. (Module 6) | Handoff — one agent explicitly transferring control (and context) to another (OpenAI Agents SDK term). (Module 7) | . Evaluation . | Eval (evaluation) — any measurement of whether a model/agent does what you want. Usually private and bespoke to your task. (Module 8) | Benchmark — a standardized, shared eval used to compare models (e.g. SWE-bench). All benchmarks are evals; most evals aren’t benchmarks. (Module 8) | Grader — the component that scores an output: programmatic (code checks), LLM-as-judge, or human. (Module 8) | LLM-as-judge — using a model to score outputs against a rubric. A fallible component you must calibrate. (Module 8) | pass@k / pass^k — succeeds in at least one of k tries (pass@k) vs. all k tries (pass^k, the reliability metric). (Module 8) | Regression eval — a fixed suite run on every change to catch silent degradation; CI for agents. (Module 8) | Contamination — a benchmark’s questions leaking into training data, inflating scores. (Module 8) | Goodhart’s law — “when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure”; overfitting to an eval set. (Module 8) | . Observability & reliability . | Trace / span — a trace is the full record of one agent run; spans are the nested steps (model calls, tool calls) within it. (Module 9) | LLM-as-judge online eval — sampling production traces and grading them continuously to catch drift. (Module 9) | Prompt caching — provider feature that caches a request’s stable prefix so repeat requests pay ~10% for the cached part. Requires an append-only, prefix-stable transcript. (Module 10) | Model tiering / routing — sending each subtask to the cheapest model that can handle it. (Module 10) | Quadratic transcript — because the whole transcript is re-sent each loop iteration, naive token cost grows ~O(n²) over a task. (Module 10) | Structured output / constrained decoding — forcing the model’s output to conform to a schema (e.g. JSON), validated at the boundary. (Modules 1, 10) | . Security . | Prompt injection — adversarial instructions hidden in data the agent reads (a web page, a file) that the model may follow; “the SQL injection of this stack.” (Module 11) | Excessive agency — giving an agent more capability/autonomy than the task needs, enlarging blast radius. (Module 11) | Permission engine — the policy layer between “model emitted a tool call” and “tool runs”: allowlists, gating, human confirmation. (Modules 3, 11) | Sandboxing — isolating tool/code execution (containers, VMs, seccomp) to limit blast radius. (Module 11) | Human-in-the-loop (HITL) — requiring human approval for high-risk or irreversible actions. (Modules 11, 12) | Guardrail — an input/output filter or check that blocks unsafe content or actions. (Module 11) | . Deployment . | Durable execution — an execution model (e.g. Temporal) that journals every step so a crashed run resumes mid-way instead of restarting. (Module 12) | Checkpointing — persisting agent state so a run can be paused/resumed/recovered (LangGraph checkpointer, etc.). (Module 12) | Long-running / persistent agent — an agent that operates over hours/days against an ongoing goal, across many context windows and sessions. (Modules 12, 13) | Background agent — an agent that runs asynchronously (often in the cloud), not in a live request/response. (Modules 12, 13) | Event-sourcing — modeling state as an append-only log of events; the natural fit for durable, resumable agents. (Module 12) | . Frontier . | Goal-directed loop / outer loop — restarting the agent against a goal repeatedly until done (vs. the inner tool loop). The “loop engineering” discourse. (Module 13) | Computer use — an agent controlling a GUI via screenshots + mouse/keyboard actions. (Module 13) | Time horizon (METR) — the length of task an agent can complete autonomously at some reliability; observed to be doubling every few months. (Module 13) | .

256.title: Resources — Canonical Reading & Tooling Index
256.content: The field moves fast. The best skill is reading primary sources. This is the curated set — favor these over secondary blog summaries.

257.title: Read these first (the canon)
257.content: . | Anthropic — Building Effective Agents (anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents). The single best starting point. Workflows vs. agents; the composable patterns (chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-worker, evaluator-optimizer). Referenced heavily in Module 6. | Anthropic — Effective Harnesses for Long-Running Agents and Harness Design for Long-Running Application Development (anthropic.com/engineering). The initializer/worker pattern, artifacts-on-disk, bridging context windows. Modules 4, 12, 13. | OpenAI — A Practical Guide to Building Agents (the OpenAI agents guide PDF). The complementary lab perspective; guardrails, the Agents SDK model. | Anthropic — Effective Context Engineering for AI Agents (engineering blog). Compaction, sub-agents, context as a managed resource. Module 4. | Chip Huyen — AI Engineering (book, 2024/25) and her blog. The best systems-level treatment of building on foundation models, incl. evals. | .

258.title: By topic
258.content: Foundations / prompting . | Anthropic prompt engineering docs (platform.claude.com/docs). Prompt caching, structured outputs, tool use. | Karpathy — Let’s build the GPT Tokenizer (YouTube) for how tokenization actually works. | . Tool use & MCP . | Model Context Protocol docs (modelcontextprotocol.io). The spec, SDKs, and the ecosystem of servers. | Provider tool-use docs (Anthropic tool use; OpenAI function calling). | . Context & memory . | Anthropic context-engineering and memory-tool docs. | Papers: Memory in the Age of AI Agents (survey); MemGPT / Letta (memory hierarchies for agents). | . Retrieval / RAG . | In Defense of RAG in the Era of Long-Context Language Models (arXiv 2409.01666) — when retrieval still wins. | Anthropic — Contextual Retrieval (engineering blog). A strong practical RAG improvement. | Search-R1 / ReSearch / DeepResearcher papers — RL-trained agentic retrieval (the frontier of RAG). | . Frameworks . | LangGraph docs (langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph) — graph state machines, checkpointing, persistence. | OpenAI Agents SDK docs — handoffs, guardrails, sessions. | Claude Agent SDK docs (platform.claude.com) — tool use, hooks, subagents, skills, MCP; and the Managed Agents surface. | CrewAI, Google ADK, Pydantic AI, Mastra (TS) — read the quickstarts to feel the design spectrum. | . Evals . | Braintrust docs & blog — eval-driven development, CI gating, trace→eval flywheel. | OpenAI Evals and Anthropic eval guidance. | SWE-bench (the canonical coding-agent benchmark) — read how a task is scored. | Hamel Husain — Your AI Product Needs Evals (blog). The practitioner classic. | . Observability . | Langfuse (open source; self-hostable), LangSmith (LangChain-native), Braintrust, Arize Phoenix, Laminar. Read each landing page + tracing quickstart. | OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions — the emerging standard for LLM/agent telemetry. | . Reliability & cost . | Provider prompt-caching docs (the economics section especially). | Provider rate-limit / batch / streaming docs. | . Security . | OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications and OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (2026) — prompt injection, excessive agency, memory poisoning, system-prompt leakage, etc. The reference for Module 11. | Simon Willison’s blog — the best ongoing writing on prompt injection (“the lethal trifecta”) and agent security. | Google — Agent security / A2A papers; SoK: The Attack Surface of Agentic AI (arXiv). | . Deployment & durable execution . | Temporal docs and their “Temporal for AI” material — durable execution for agents (used by OpenAI Codex, Replit, etc.). | LangGraph persistence/checkpointing docs; LangGraph Platform. | Anthropic Managed Agents docs — a hosted approach to running the loop + sandbox. | . Frontier / long-running . | METR — Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks (the time-horizon-doubling result). | Geoffrey Huntley — Ralph Wiggum as a “software engineer” (the outer-loop meme) and HumanLayer’s A Brief History of Ralph. | Computer-use docs (Anthropic computer use; OpenAI computer-using-agent). | .

260.title: How to keep up
260.content: . | Follow the engineering blogs of Anthropic, OpenAI, LangChain, and the eval/observability vendors. | Read METR’s evaluations for capability trends. | When a new framework/tool trends, read its quickstart and its “why” page, then map it onto the concepts in this course — you’ll usually find it’s a repackaging of patterns you already know. | .
